This video can not be played Watch: Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution  India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday. Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors. Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October. Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy. The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.  But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business. More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition âfrom Musk. For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution, spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy. Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed. Jio's cheap tariffs democratised internet use in India a decade ago This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband. Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India". But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs. "The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management. "A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholdersâ¦ which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed." Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note. The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede. "The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind". For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available. While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services. India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones. Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise. All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user. "Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global. The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.  At $3.2bn, the Jio Platforms IPO is India's biggest share sale But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades. The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors. Dhirubhai Ambani, the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s. In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company. And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence. "The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC. "That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."  Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external. News Americans could spend over $4 billion on Halloween candy this year. Writer Writer  				Edited by Gael Cooper  October 27, 2026, 5:58 pm ET If you can’t afford a trip to a haunted house this spooky season, just swing by the supermarket candy aisle for a nasty scare. The price of sweets jumped over the last few years, soaring even faster than the average inflation rate, according to a recent report from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, with higher ingredient costs as the primary villain. October is important for candy sales, as shoppers stock up for parties, trick-or-treaters, or — let’s be honest — personal consumption. “The biggest purchasing days are still ahead, with about 35% of Halloween seasonal sales expected this week,” a Hershey Company spokesperson told CNET. More from CNET Chocolate treats have become especially expensive, as a recent global cocoa shortage squeezed the market while candy companies were preparing shipments for Halloween.  But despite chilling prices, chocolate is still making its way into Halloween bags and buckets.  “Trick-or-treat participation intent is in line with last year,” the Hershey spokesperson said. “Confection remains a resilient category.” Americans will likely spend over $13 billion on Halloween this year, the National Retail Federation reports. That’s almost twice the $6.9 billion people spent on the holiday 11 years ago, in 2015. “Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind,” Allison Zeller, a National Retail Federation vice president, said in a statement.  Candy remains the favorite purchase, with 95% of Halloween shoppers planning to snag some this year, followed by decorations, costumes and greeting cards, according to the National Retail Federation. In 2026, shoppers are expected to spend over $4 billion on Halloween candy alone. An Oct. 20 report from research group Groundwork Collaborative broke down which candy prices have risen the most this year. The Mondelez Sour Gummy Candy variety pack, which jumped 39% in price, and Hershey seasonal Peanut Butter Cups, which saw a 23% increase, are this year’s most expensive Halloween candy compared with last season.  The squeeze doesn’t stop in the candy aisle — utility bills and other essentials are climbing, too. A Consumer Reports survey from earlier this month found that one in five American families has cut back on groceries due to rising energy costs.  “If you’ve been waiting until now to get your Halloween goodies, you’re right to do so. Halloween sales hit the high street and online two or three days before Halloween as stores try to clear stock,” says James Bricknell, CNET commerce managing editor. “If you’re all set for this year, do what I did last year and grab a bunch of costumes and decorations the day after Halloween,” he adds. “Then, you can store them ready to go for Halloween 2027.”   		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Alex Mayyasi                        The discount grocery chain Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028.                                                           Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America                                       hide caption  In the summer of 2020, I lived briefly in Ithaca, New York. It's the only time I've lived near Aldi, the grocery store known for low prices. I went twice, and I thought it was fine, but underwhelming. I appreciated the low prices, but it didn't have everything I needed. The store was small and a bit shabby. I didn't know it yet, but those are the exact ingredients that have made Aldi the fastest-growing grocery chain in America. Per Bloomberg, Aldi plans to have more than 3,000 American locations by the end of 2028, which would be more than any other chain but Walmart. In 2024, Aldi generated some $29 billion in U.S. sales, which is more than Trader Joe's. Aldi is a German company known for having low, low prices, and it deserves that reputation. Food reporter Deena Shanker told me for my podcast Gastronomics that her experience comparison shopping over many months was that Aldi either matched Walmart on price or was a bit cheaper. Grocers like Wegmans and Kroger have announced defensive price reductions, and an analysis published in late 2023 of Lidl, another German grocer with a very similar model to Aldi's but fewer U.S. stores, found that grocery chains reduced their markups ~7 percent in areas where Lidl stores opened. All to say: Aldi is disrupting the grocery business and actually lowering prices even as the cost of food—at restaurants and other grocery stores—goes up and up. Maybe this sounds a bit humdrum. But I found it totally intriguing and perplexing, because… One necessary but not sufficient explanation for Aldi's low prices is that management is obsessed with efficiency and cutting unnecessary costs. There's no music in stores, because speakers (and licensing fees for muzak) cost money. The staff places products on shelves still in the cardboard boxes they were trucked in on, because artfully unpacking fruits, bread, and jerky sticks would mean higher labor costs. The shabbiness is intentional — it's the cost of cheaper groceries. But other grocery chains are similarly obsessed with efficiency. Here's one of my favorite examples about Costco, courtesy of Zachary Crockett and The Hustle: "In another instance, reengineering a container of cashews from a circle to a square shape allowed Costco to stack more items in a single truck, reducing the number of shipments by 24,000 pallets per year. For shoppers, this meant cheaper nuts." Instead, Aldi's disruptively low prices rely on two primary tactics: Aldi's low prices made their stores very attractive during periods like the Great Recession and today's inflationary era. The Great Recession, especially, enabled their current growth. But if all Aldi offered was bargain prices in shabby stores, customers might flee to Costco, Kroger, or Whole Foods when the economy recovered. So another key to Aldi's success is that it's fun. Aldi has a famously chaotic-good middle aisle with rotating buys like fun toys, German spätzle, and advent calendars that contain 24 festive cheeses. And its U.S. stores have expanded their offerings (a bit) to attract higher-income customers: Aldi doesn't just have the cheapest apples, but the cheapest honey crisp apples. Not just super-duper cheap wine but well-priced "premium" wine. Instead of being a sad place to shop when you're low on cash, Aldi has more flea-market energy: a place anyone might go to hunt for good deals and fun finds. Aldi is beloved; many customers arecult-like in their devotion. In some cases, customers line up for new store openings like early iPhone releases. My main takeaway from researching and analyzing Aldi for several weeks (foran episode of Gastronomics!) is that there's always something new under the sun. American grocery stores are a mature market. They seem pretty stable equilibrium-y. But they are dynamic and always changing. Aldi didn't need futuristic tech to disrupt the industry; just a strategy developed 80 years ago, then tweaked for the American market. In healthy markets, there's always a way in for new competitors. My other takeaway is greater appreciation for the famous business idiom: "There are only two ways to make money in business: One is to bundle; the other is to unbundle." The clearest example of bundling and unbundling is probably television. Cable companies bundled hundreds of TV channels together and charged one high fee for all of them. Then streaming services like Netflix made money by unbundling television — by allowing people to pay for just Netflix. Which felt liberating! For a few years. But now customers are annoyed about subscribing to so many streaming services. So streamers are teaming up to form bundles, like getting Disney, Hulu, and HBO Max all for one reduced price. Now, to make money, you gotta bundle. Even the person who coined the phrase about bundling and unbundling didn't think it's literally the only way to make money. Still, I often failed to see (un)bundling as a powerful framework outside of the media industry. Until I realized that Aldi is unbundling the grocery store. For a long time, grocery stores got more bundled. People once went to the baker, the butcher, and the greengrocer. Then the super market put all those things under one roof. And then Walmart, Target, and Costco created superstores where you could buy groceries and clothes and big-screen TVs. Now Aldi is reversing this process by unbundling the grocery store. Not only does Aldi not have the big-screen TVs and dupes of Lululemon hoodies and pants, it doesn't even have everything on your grocery list. Aldi unbundled the part of the grocery business it can do super cheaply, and it intentionally locates Aldi stores near competitor grocery stores so shoppers can easily go grab the last few things on their list (the rest of the bundle). With this in mind, I've started seeing bundling and unbundling at work in more and more industries. If you look closely at your own, I suspect you will, too. My third takeaway is that I just didn't live in Ithaca long enough to grok Aldi. If I'd been there longer, I bet I would have made Aldi part of a multi-store strategy. I get it now! Aldi, please come to Colorado (where I live)! At the start of this post, I asked three questions inspired by Aldi's expansion. The first two, which are about how Aldi achieved a comparative advantage, I feel like I've answered. The third was whether the American economy can still deliver a bounty of affordable food. I think the way Aldi's growth pressured competitors to keep prices low shows that grocers are not the right target of our ire over food prices. But grocery stores are just one slice of the food world. Alex Mayyasi is the author of the best-selling book, Planet Money: A Guide to the Economic Forces That Shape Your Life. He writes a Substack newsletter and hosts the podcast Gastronomics about the business of food and how economics shapes what we eat. This wasn't your usual S-1 filing. Most are drab financial documents: revenue, liabilities, risk factors. Line after line. Page after page. Anthropic did something different. It wrote its own Good Book, BI's Henry Chandonnet writes. Anthropic's S-1 reads less like an IPO filing with the SEC than a dispatch from a heavenly mountaintop: the gospel according to Claude. Seeking salvation for humanity and a blockbuster stock-market listing. Both, apparently, can fit on the same form. The language suggests Anthropic isn't merely asking investors to believe it can make money. It asks them to believe in a mission grand enough to make its enormous AI spending look like a necessary cost. That is the story Anthropic will soon take to Wall Street. At a potential $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation, Anthropic could become the largest IPO ever — just as investors fret that an already wobbly AI trade may struggle to absorb another colossus. Beneath the biblical flourishes, the filing also answers one of the biggest questions hanging over the AI boom, BI's Alistair Barr writes: Can AI labs actually make money? Yes, and potentially lots of it.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    It is a remarkable document. Lucky for you, we've read its 300-plus pages and 259,031 words. Here are the key revelations. The congregation is not quite of one mind. Some investors see astonishing growth. Others see hundreds of billions of dollars in future compute commitments. See what smart people are saying about Anthropic's IPO paperwork. Every doctrine needs an early believer. For Anthropic, that was Spark Capital. The firm appears more than 50 times in the S-1 because partner Yasmin Razavi sits on Anthropic's board; Spark led the company's $450 million Series C at a then-eye-watering $4.5 billion valuation in 2023. That early faith looks set to be well-rewarded. Anthropic's seven cofounders are also poised to become extraordinarily wealthy when the company goes public. We're talking tens of billions of dollars. In the next few weeks, public investors will finally get their chance to buy a piece of Anthropic, too. But they should be aware: Anthropic wants public money, not much public input. Its founders will have 50.1% of the voting power, while a trust created and funded by the company has the ability to appoint four of its seven directors. Inside the company, meanwhile, there is life among the believers. Anthropic's own workforce offers a glimpse of how Claude is reshaping the company from within, as it rapidly grows headcount and tries to build a "low-ego" culture. And finally, a question worthy of theological debate: Did AI help write its own scripture? Business Insider put Anthropic's filing through an AI-writing detector. Here's what we found. Jump to

Apple yesterday officially launched what it describes as “the biggest update ever” to the iPad mini, featuring an OLED screen and a thinner, lighter design. However, while there are a significant number of upgrades, internet commentators were very focused on the one thing Apple didn’t upgrade: that 60Hz display …  Apple highlighted the new features. A stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance. The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience. A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support. Commenters, however, were quick to point to the fact that the refresh rate wasn’t mentioned, with the obvious conclusion that it remains 60Hz instead of being updated to a ProMotion variable refresh rate of 1 to 120Hz. “700 bucks and no 120hz display?” “I was someone interested in adding a mini but at 60hz, 128gb, no Face ID I can’t justify the already inflated price tag.” “60Hz right? in 2026 right? Hell no.” “60Hz? Next…” “60Hz in 2026. Apple should be ashamed.” At the price they're asking, it should have ProMotion and Face ID. Don't care about Apple's reasons for raising the price, it doesn't affect consumers' perceived value of the iPad Mini. I could include many more quotes, but you get the idea. It’s certainly a surprising omission in a 2026 device, especially when our sister site 9to5Google noted that the closest Android competitor has a 185Hz refresh rate. The biggest point in Redmagic’s favor is in that display, too. Where Apple is still refusing to give the iPad Mini a 120Hz refresh rate with this latest model – utterly insane in the year two thousand and twenty-six, if I do say so myself – Astra 2 has a 185Hz refresh rate. I’ve not found that inherently better than a standard 120Hz panel, but it’s way better than the 60Hz panel Apple’s latest will still be using. Now I fully acknowledge that Apple knows the iPad mini market better than any of us do. I’m also aware that it has historically been primarily a business device, used for applications ranging from restaurant waitstaff relaying orders to the kitchen through mobile payment terminals to warehouse inventory systems. None of these types of applications would remotely benefit from a display with a faster refresh rate. Additionally, when it comes to consumers, I’m sure it’s true that not everyone appreciates the benefits of 120Hz. Some of those in our comments claimed they couldn’t tell the difference, while others said it was only really relevant to gaming. Adding that category of individual purchasers to the majority business market, and Apple has undoubtedly correctly concluded that the majority of its customers simply don’t care about this feature.  However … Those who do care about it, care about it rather a lot. I don’t know what the unit cost difference would be, but since 120Hz is now standard on a great many cheaper devices, I can’t imagine it’s a substantial one. I can’t help feeling that this is a case where Apple simply should have done the right thing, even if only a minority of buyers would appreciate it.  FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. Tech > Services & Software > AI Companies are accused of training their AI models using copyrighted music and lyrics.  				Edited by Gael Cooper  October 27, 2026, 5:22 pm ET The Man in Black couldn’t have imagined this. AI companies Suno and Anthropic face a combined $338 million in lawsuits for allegedly using songs and lyrics by Madonna, Johnny Cash and Joni Mitchell to train their artificial intelligence systems. Reservoir Media Management, a music rights company, filed two separate lawsuits on Oct. 21. In one of them, Reservoir accuses Suno of scraping 1,050 copyrighted songs — including Cash’s Ring of Fire, Mitchell’s Both Sides Now and Madonna’s Papa Don’t Preach. Suno is a platform where users can generate an AI song using only a text prompt. In the other lawsuit, Reservoir accuses Anthropic of using copyrighted lyrics from 853 songs to train its Claude family of AI models. Some of the songs mentioned in that lawsuit include Mitchell’s Big Yellow Taxi, Billy Strayhorn’s Lush Life and Evanescence‘s Bring Me to Life. More from CNET “We disagree with the allegations and intend to defend this case vigorously,” a representative for Anthropic told Billboard. Representatives for Suno and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Reservoir seeks $186.4 million in damages from Suno and $151.4 million from Anthropic. Both lawsuits accuse the companies of copyright infringement, circumventing restrictions such as logins and paywalls and stripping song credits of title, writer and publisher data. Anthropic was also sued last week for violating copyright for reportedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train Claude. The company has been sued more than a dozen times for copyright infringement — most notably in a $1.5 billion settlement over allegations that it trained its AI on millions of pirated books. Suno also faces several copyright infringement lawsuits, including a second from Sony Music and Universal Music Group. Reservoir founder and CEO Golnar Khosrowshahi told Music Business Worldwide that the AI music industry can’t be allowed to exploit songwriters’ work. “When we believe their work has been exploited without authorization, we will hold AI platforms legally accountable to ensure those rights are upheld,” Khosrowshahi said. “We will continue to advocate for a framework that supports technological progress while protecting the creative work at the heart of our industry.” Copyright infringement — of news articles, music, books and art  — has become a major issue, with several AI companies accused of ingesting mountains of data to train AI models such as Claude, OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s Gemini and Elon Musk’s Grok. There’s even a website, the AI Lawsuit Tracker, that counts 145 copyright infringement lawsuits — more than half of the overall cases against AI companies. AI models are trained when their companies feed a vast amount of data — text, images, music, videos and software code — into their AI systems. With all that data, as well as synthetic data generated by computers, AI models can learn to generate words, images and video that may appear human-created. In the lawsuit filed last week, Reservoir said Suno has already admitted to copying “essentially all music files of reasonable quality that are accessible on the open internet,” a statement Suno made in court during a 2024 suit brought by Universal Music Group, Sony Music Entertainment, and Warner Music Group. This summer, a hacker cracked into Suno’s code and revealed that the company allegedly scraped music and lyrics from platforms like YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius and stock music libraries. The hack showed more than 2 million clips in a folder called “youtube_music,” as well as thousands of hours of music from the lyrics database Genius HQ, the music streaming service Deezer, and the stock music site Pond5. In the lawsuit, Reservoir says that Suno is not truly a platform for people to create music and “was instead always meant to replace the artists whose works were being unlawfully copied by directly reaching those artists’ listeners with AI-generated substitutes which copy the originals.” Reservoir also accused Anthropic of using a text-extraction tool called Newspaper, which removes copyright notices from written material. Reservoir said Claude is partly trained on lyrics collected from Common Crawl, a web crawler that, during its crawls, inadvertently picks up lyrics from licensed sites such as Musixmatch and LyricFind.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. Login  Vlad  27 October 2026   Samsung Android Apple vivo Xiaomi iQOO Poco iOS Oppo OnePlus  Last week, Omdia reported that India's smartphone shipments dropped 26% in Q3 to their lowest level since 2016. Now Counterpoint Research has published its own numbers, and while they're a bit less dire, they paint the same picture. Shipments apparently fell 20% year-on-year in July-September, to their lowest level in a decade. Unsurprisingly, record-high memory prices are to blame, since they drove up device costs. With demand staying soft, brands also kept less stock in stores, even ahead of the festive season. The cheaper end of the market took the hardest hit. Shipments of phones under INR 20,000 ($210) declined by 47%, as rising prices pushed models into higher price bands. Counterpoint says the pressure was especially strong below INR 15,000 ($158), with consumers holding on to their phones for longer and putting off upgrades. Samsung reclaimed the top spot after nine quarters with a 17% share, thanks to its Galaxy A series and relatively measured price hikes. vivo (excluding iQOO) was a close second with 16%. Oppo came in third with 12%, driven by triple-digit growth above INR 20,000 ($210). Xiaomi (including Poco) was fourth, also with 12%, and it was the top brand in the INR 10,001-20,000 ($105-$210) band. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro series got off to a strong start, with initial sales nearly 20% higher than those of the iPhone 17 Pro family. Ai+ Smartphone was the fastest-growing brand, with shipments up 306%, and Indian brands as a whole went from a 2% share to 7%. itel grew 88%, and Google was up over 50%, helped by the Pixel 11 devices. On the chipset side, MediaTek stayed on top with a 45% share, while Unisoc saw a resurgence as brands focused on making more profit in the lower price segments. Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects India's smartphone market to shrink by around 13% in 2026, with another round of price hikes likely after the festive season sale. Brands are already reacting by launching more 4G and lower-spec models in the mass market, and the firm thinks 2027 will be challenging as well. So if you were hoping for prices to come back down soon, definitely don't hold your breath. Last month, Twelve South introduced the wildly popular AirFly Drive, its first wireless CarPlay adapter (which is now back in stock after initially selling out).  Now, the popular accessory maker is back with Airfly View, which adds a built-in screen to its other popular wireless audio dongle. You can order it on Amazon today. Here’s how it works.  For those unfamiliar, Twelve South’s Airfly accessory is a popular choice among travelers. It lets you connect your AirPods or other Bluetooth headphones to the seat-back entertainment screen on a plane, even if that screen doesn’t support Bluetooth natively. And while it’s particularly popular among travelers, it actually can make a headphone jack wireless just about anywhere.   The new Airfly View builds on the Airfly foundation by adding a built-in screen. The screen makes it easier to set up Airfly, guiding you through the process with on-screen prompts. Airfly View offers up to 16 hours of battery life, and the screen makes it easy to know when it’s time to charge.  Twelve South explains:  Airfly View shows each step of pairing on its own display, in any of 24 languages, whether that happens at home the night before or at the gate before boarding. On the plane, plug it into the seatback jack and the screen shows which headphones are connected and how much battery is left, then turns off when it is not in use.  More Airfly View features:  You can order the new Airfly View on Amazon today for $79.99 in black and coastal color options. As a child, you may have sung along to Toys R Us' iconic jingle about not wanting to grow up. Decades later, many millennial and Gen Z adults are taking that motto seriously. Adults are rediscovering how Lego, stuffed animals, and other toys brought them joy. Now that they're earning their own money, they can afford the things they once played with or circled in catalogs. Hobby spending — which includes hobby shops, arts and crafts stores, and outdoor recreation providers — rose 7.9% year over year in August, according to an analysis by the Bank of America Institute. Devin Byron, 25, had a collection of American Girl dolls growing up, but her interest in playing with them fizzled out around middle school. However, her love for them never really went away. And now, working an office job, she can buy her own. In February, she and her friend went to the American Girl store in New York. Byron purchased the historical doll representing the '60s, Melody, which cost $135 with the book, plus $34 for accessories. "I feel like a lot of collectors now are, I would say, healing their inner child because some people couldn't get maybe American Girl dolls growing up, but now they can," Byron said. "And it's an adrenaline rush too." She's not the only adult contributing to the toy economy. Market research company Circana found that adult-only households made up over half of toy sales in the first half of this year, and that overall toy sales for adults increased 25%. Some adults may buy toys to bring nostalgia back into their lives or to avoid doomscrolling. For others, it's to make a profit. "We're seeing toys increasingly function as hobbies, fandom ecosystems, and social experiences rather than traditional children's products," said Kristen McLean, vice president of client insights for Circana's Entertainment Knowledge Group. "That's expanding the consumer base and creating new opportunities for manufacturers and retailers that understand how to engage collectors, enthusiasts, gifters, and self-purchasers." Jay Berino, store manager at the Lowry Town Center Timbuk Toys in Denver, pointed to "kidulting," the trend in which adults engage with childlike toys and hobbies, as coming from adults seeking distractions and nostalgia — from buying Pokémon cards to lava lamps. "As much as we're a toy store and people hear toy store and think of kids, we sell to a lot to full-blown adults, and that drives a huge chunk of our business," he said. Syls Farmer, 32, runs a vintage online store specializing in toys marketed to girls. Her store, Mema's Doll Shop, was inspired by her grandmother, who ran a couple of toy stores back in the day. Farmer said adults buy from her for themselves or for their kids so they can experience their past. "A lot of people are dealing with a lot of pressure in this general economy and the world in general," Farmer said. "And I think that these items of childhood are bringing back feelings of comfort and peace that I think a lot of us need right now." Farmer also buys toys for herself, including her first American Girl doll through Facebook Marketplace — Nicki, one of the '90s-inspired dolls.   Even crafters are getting in on the toy craze: Abby Glassenberg, the president of the Craft Industry Alliance, said that homemade Labubu-esque bag charms have taken off, with crafters making their own customizable charms from crochet or felt. "People are definitely still spending. I think craft in some ways is resistant to market up and down," Glassenberg said. When the market is up, people pour more money into their hobbies, whether that's getting premium materials or even traveling to somewhere catered to their favorite crafts. "When the market is down, and people's budgets are tighter, they want to make something for a gift rather than buy it," Glassenberg said. Emma Wynn, 28, has 120 Jellycat items, a popular stuffed-toy brand that includes animals, food, and more. Wynn's collection began when she bought a scuba diver egg while browsing at a garden center with her family, sparking a feeling of childlike happiness. Prices range on the Jellycat site; for instance, a heart dragon is priced at $80, a carrot cake is priced at $45, and bear winter decorations are priced at $28. Wynn funds her collection with money she earns from content creation, rather than from her corporate job. Wynn thinks adults buy toys because they bring back happy childhood memories, can provide a dopamine hit when someone finds something they've been searching for a while, and can connect them with others who are building similar collections. "It feels very empowering to be unapologetic about the things that bring us joy and happiness, whereas before maybe I would've been embarrassed about it," she said. It can also be a tangible way to remember a memory. For instance, Wynn's soon-to-be mother-in-law bought her a Jellycat flower bouquet to celebrate her new engagement. Harrison Woodward, 28, said building and playing with Lego sets was a large part of his childhood. For one birthday in his early 20s, his aunt bought him a Lego Porsche car model, reigniting his passion for Lego sets. He put on a streaming show after a long day of work and started to build the over 1,000-piece product. "It was just the most therapeutic, peaceful activity," he said. "You could sit there for a few hours, a few days in a row, and complete a set and see it come together and marvel at all the different engineering things that they put into these sets now." He left his job in insurance to focus on content creation full time. He posts about his Lego collection and passion for cars; he recently started collecting Hot Wheels, another childhood favorite. He has spent thousands on Lego and is running out of space in a room that's filled with his collections. He still tries to find a balance so that building isn't just for content, such as taking his time to build a CaDA car set in the evening. Woodward thinks adults might be purchasing toys to invest some time in their hobbies and take care of their mental health. "I think the stigma has kind of lifted over collecting and everything," he said. "I think that for a long time people thought any of this stuff was strictly for kids, but as the years have gone on and adults have continued to adopt it, the stigma continues to go further and further away." Trading cards have also become a major area of interest for some adults. Kian Golshan previously told Business Insider that Pokémon is a lucrative side hustle. For instance, he sold a Japanese-edition Charmander for $750 that he bought for $59.26. As Business Insider's Samuel O'Brient previously reported, Golshan was able to put the analytical skills that he developed while working in finance to work. "It helps me kind of think through the risks and when to take profits, when to sell, what to hold, what's my like risk profile, what's tracking the market," Golshan said. Byron, the Gen Zer who bought an American doll, still has her collection of dolls from her childhood. Plus, she has her most recent addition displayed in her room. "I'm actually thinking about going back to the store again," she said. "Maybe I'll walk out with another doll. I guess we'll see." Jump to

The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro is an excellent "premium" controller with top-tier ergonomics, functionality, specs, and versatility. It's unfortunate that it misses out on some typical premium features like a charging dock or Bluetooth, but it makes up for it with razor-sharp (pun intended) focus on the fundamentals.  Rock-solid signal delivery, a big improvement Capacitive anti-drift sticks with great action Superb ergonomics, buttons, and inputs, complete with trigger locks Great customization and software No charging dock option, unlike other similarly priced premium controllers Lacks Bluetooth support Sound-based haptics aren't consistent  Why you can trust Windows Central     Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.  The Razer Wolverine has been the torchbearer for premium alternative Xbox controllers for some time. And now we're on iteration V4, which was released just a few weeks ago. It comes at an interesting time for the best Xbox controllers. Microsoft relinquished exclusivity over its Xbox Wireless signal. In previous years, all third-party Xbox controllers were wired, which was irritating to say the least, especially since Xbox refused to use new tech like haptics or anti-drift capacitivate thumbsticks. That might be changing with the Xbox Elite Series 3, rumored to be imminent for release, but it's not here yet. Between then and now, we still have the Razer Wolverine V4 Pro, which might just be the best Xbox controller I've ever used — even if it is missing some crucial features on the convenience side. But for how long will it remain the king? And is it really worth the cash?      The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro is a powerhouse when it comes to raw specs, offering a truly absurd 8,000 Hz maximum polling rate on PC. It's limited to 250 Hz on Xbox (owing to Microsoft's Xbox Wireless signal), but for those who truly want some e-sports-grade connectivity on Windows PC, you need look no further. Specification Razer Wolverine V4 Pro  Compatibility Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, Windows PC Connectivity Razer HyperSpeed Wireless (2.4 GHz), USB-C wired Polling Rate Up to 8,000 Hz on PC, up to 250 Hz on Xbox Thumbsticks High-resolution capacitive anti-drift thumbsticks with interchangeable stick caps Additional Inputs 4 removable rear buttons and 2 claw-grip bumpers (6 extra inputs total) Triggers With locks for adjustable short-throw and full-range modes Customization Remappable controls, interchangeable thumbstick caps, removable faceplate, 4 onboard profiles Battery Life Up to 27 hours Price $199.99 MSRP The Xbox version is only compatible with Xbox consoles and Windows PCs, sadly lacking Bluetooth for anyone who wants something compatible with mobile devices on the side. It comes with a USB dongle in the box with Razer's high-spec polling rate capabilities and dynamic switching between Xbox and PC. No need to flip a switch on the dongle itself anymore. The thumbsticks are capacitive and thus anti-drift (a major issue with all current Xbox controllers), and measures far more steps than typical TMR sticks. They come with programmable "claw" shoulder buttons as well as four removable back buttons, Elite-style. It sports up to 27 hours of continuous play, is chargeable via USB-C cable, and has a removable faceplate for good measure. It all comes in at $199.99, however, putting it on par with the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller with its full bundle of accessories. While you do miss out on a charge dock and Bluetooth, you are gaining some serious firepower and a design chassis built to last, rather than fall apart.      The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro is becoming something of a leader in this space. I've been using the Razer Wolverine V3 Pro as my go-to PC gaming controller for some time now, and to say I'm used to it would be an understatement. I would say I've come to prefer it overall, particularly over time, as my Xbox Elite Controller Series 2 has succumbed to stick drift in a big, annoying way. But more on that in a sec. The Wolverine V4 Pro doesn't reinvent the wheel over its predecessors, but does address some nitpicks and annoyances I've seen some people have. It comes with the same two extra shoulder claw bumpers, which can be programmed to do a variety of additional things. The back paddles can be removed now, for those who prefer to only rock two instead of all four, for example. The buttons and D-pad still have a "clicky" actuation, which I know sometimes gets a mixed reaction. I don't mind it myself, but if you didn't like it, know that it's back here with the V4.      The sticks are capacitive anti-drift, and contactless, and should be utterly resistant against wear and tear. Quality-wise, they feel almost 1:1 with what Xbox offers — minus the inevitable drift, which is a huge plus. Razer includes some swappable options in the box too, and they're easy to swap out. Unlike the magnetic ones on the Elite, though, Razer's won't fall off as easily, as they're held in place with a small clasp. I can't tell you how many times I've dropped my Elite controller only for the thumbsticks to fall off and go hiding somewhere. Design-wise, the Razer Wolverine V4 Pro is not exactly a huge looker, but it does have a magnetic faceplate that can be swapped out for custom designs. I've not seen any available online yet, but I'm sure they're coming down the pipeline. I'm not a huge fan of the large USB-C port on the top of the controller, which juts out haphazardly. It's not a big deal, and I guess it helps hold the cable in place for charging, but it isn't a pretty solution. Speaking of charging, the Razer Wolverine V4 Pro gets around 27 hours on a single charge according to the firm, although I'd say it clocks in a bit less than that in practice, maybe around 20-24 hours when used via Xbox. Coupled with the fact that it has no charge dock unlike other controllers in this price range, I was hoping Razer would look to move beyond cables with the V4 Pro. Alas, we might need to wait for the V5. Again, not a big deal, but it is something worth considering.      Razer's software is still among the best third-party solutions for gaming accessories on PC, in my view, with everything bundled in a single place. It's easy to manage the features on the Wolverine V4, assigning buttons and the like, although be wary of using Razer's macros in some competitive games — automation detection can get you banned in some PvP titles like shooters. Offline though, it can be a handy feature, especially in some management and simulation games. Speaking of shooters, Razer's triggers are also well put together here. The trigger locks make activation more rapid, which can be a boost for pistols and rifle fire. You can disable them with a switch for full motion activation for acceleration in racing games and things like that. The V4 boasts flawless reception without disconnects or degradation, even in a radio-hostile environment. Crucially, Razer also seems to have eliminated signal interference issues that came in the box with the V3. Firmware updates fixed those over time, but the V4 boasts flawless reception without disconnects or degradation, even in a radio-hostile environment (i.e., my office with a thousand other radio signals interfering with each other). All in all, I think this is more of a refinement and iteration over the V3 Pro, improving and polishing the strong fundamentals to a mirror finish.      There are many great Xbox controllers from third-party firms these days. As much as I truly adore the convenience of the Xbox Elite charge dock and monstrous, infinite-feeling battery, the sticks and general build quality degrade rapidly over time. It's hard to recommend the Xbox Elite controller these days to most people as a result, even if the dock is the best out there by a mile. The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro is not cheap at $199, and perhaps is best considered over things like 8BitDo Ultimate 3E if you are looking for something on the higher end for rapid response in multiplayer PvP PC games, like Call of Duty and such. The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Xbox / PC wireless controller has a charge dock, has Bluetooth, as well as anti-drift sticks and programmable additional buttons. It is also $70 cheaper than the Razer Wolverine V4 Pro, at the cost of a "premium feel" potentially. Razer also rocks that absurd 8000 Hz maximum polling, although the 8BitDo does also go up to 1000 Hz on PC for good measure, albeit with a smaller battery. I wish Razer would jump on the battery dock train to reduce reliance on cables and charging. I shouldn't need to be scrambling for a cable mid-match in 2026, particularly when so many others are offering them now. There are also even more premium options out there now too, like the SteelSeries Aeon Pro, which is $50 more expensive, but also offers a charge dock and the ability to connect and switch between two platforms at once. The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro asks you to physically move the dongle between platforms if you're moving between devices, which isn't always ideal either.      I think the 8000 Hz polling radio does a lot of the heavy lifting on the price here, potentially making this a niche option for esports-grade level play — something other controllers simply don't offer right now. However, for the vast majority of consumers, I would've liked to have seen a bit more on the convenience end. This is branded as a "Pro" controller, though to be fair, i.e. for "Pro" gamers. In that, it does exactly the job it set out to do. There are other options that might be better value for a regular gamer like those outlined above. There's also the Xbox Elite Controller Series 3 which is probably just weeks away from a reveal, making the decision to grab this even murkier maybe in the near term (as of writing, that is). But one thing is for sure: you won't be disappointed if you do end up picking this controller up. The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro absolutely nails the fundamentals like few other controllers do, delivering massive performance in a tidy, intuitive package.           The Razer Wolverine V4 Pro is a stellar controller that every other controller should draw from with regards to the fundamentals. Superb ergonomics, great customizability, and high-quality materials provide a reassuring sense of value for money. As a consumer, I'd probably swap out the 8K polling for something else, but this is for "Pro" gamers, and in that, it surely delivers. Sweetgreen restaurant managers are about to see some more sweet green. The salad bowl chain said Tuesday it is rolling out a new compensation and incentive plan for the new year that would raise annual pay for managers of high-performing locations to more than $200,000. "This sets Sweetgreen up to be in the top tier of restaurants for total compensation for general managers," chief operating officer Jason Cochran told Business Insider. "Our ability to be able to attract, retain, and also inspire many of our internal team members to want to be head coaches — I think it's going to be meaningful for many years to come." Managers need to have at least three years on the job to be eligible for the highest pay bands, and a new revenue-share bonus will directly reward leaders when their location beats it sales goals, the company said. Managers may also receive shares of Sweetgreen stock based on their performance. Cochran said the typical tenure of restaurant managers ranges from three months to 10 years, and that store teams consist of about 25 to 50 employees. "One of the shift leads was telling me they heard the news and how excited they were for their career at Sweetgreen," he said. "She's been with us six years." The company also said the changes at the top are part of a larger push to improve talent retention and training within the chain. "Great leaders build great teams, and great teams build a great business. As we approach 300 restaurants, we're betting big on our Head Coaches," co-founder and CEO Jonathan Nemen said in a statement. "The restaurant industry has always been one of the great engines of opportunity, and we want to make that real for thousands of people." Jump to

The maker of miracles may no longer be God, but it does rhyme with him.  Anthropic, creator of Claude, filed its S-1 paperwork on Monday in preparation for a gargantuan initial public offering. The document runs over 300 pages and spans more than 240,000 words, some 50,000 more than the New Testament. It asks potential investors to prioritize mission over money: "Mission" appears 79 times, while "money" — the thing an S-1 is filed to generate, in this case, a bajillion dollars worth — a mere 17. The company professes it could "bend the arc of geopolitical history toward freedom"; it could grow economies everywhere, including "the poorer parts of the world"; it could cure "diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia." Page 4 of the S-1 is not dissimilar from Jesus in Matthew 11: "The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them." Anthropic aims to "bring forth an age of miracles," it writes, and the investors who buy in should be true believers. Because in the wrong hands, as you'll see if you turn your missals to page 46, AI can be built in ways that pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." While S-1s are definitionally visions of the future and full of hype, most are drab financial documents, eye-popping for their prospective profits more than their prose. But Anthropic didn't just open up its book; it wrote its own Good Book, a Bible-like statement of good and evil that joins a growing canon of the company's sacred texts. If you were to stumble onto any random page of this S-1, you'd be forgiven for thinking you were reading not a perfunctory government filing but the scripture of a doomsday religion. Anthropic has long dodged allegations of fomenting a new, questionable faith. Headlines and takes on Anthropic's cultishness abound: "The Cult of Anthropic" (The Information), "Anthropic is a Cult and Claude is rapidly becoming its God" (The New York Post), "Has a cult ever started a company as successful as Anthropic?" (Peter "Beware the Antichrist" Thiel). Critics point to the employees' extinction predictions — p(doom) is not too far from p(rapture) — and ties to the effective altruism movement. It doesn't help that Dario Amodei was reportedly a Y2K prepper in high school. Anthropic has welcomed the reputation in other ways, inviting religious leaders to oversee the construction of Claude's rules. In its S-1, Anthropic asks investors to take an actual leap of faith. Let's play: Is that an Anthropic core value or one of God's 10 commandments? Anthropic asks its employees to act for the "global good," be "helpful, honest, and harmless," and "hold light and shade." They shall have no other gods — as in, "put the mission first." And, just as followers must sublimate themselves to praise God, Anthropic employees must be "low-ego." The S-1 says it at least nine times. To understand Anthropic, you'll need to understand 42 ornate terms. The S-1's glossary is sprawling, including neologisms for virtuous acts ("closing the loop") and evil deeds ("prompt injection"). Then there's "Constitutional AI," a type of large language model that is trained with goodness in mind. The SEC's "Plain English Handbook" implores companies to use "concrete, everyday words" and to avoid "relying on glossaries and defined terms." But can you truly be AGI-pilled if you don't speak of "interleaved thinking," "mechanistic interpretability," or "multi-agent orchestration"? It's exceedingly hard to get a job at Anthropic, and not just because of the massive pool of cash-eyed engineers seeking IPO windfalls. The company has an intensive interview process, one it name-checks in the S-1. It looks for honesty, trust, and (you guessed it) a low ego. "We are willing to turn down candidates who don't demonstrate them, even if they are extremely strong technically," the S-1 reads. They must, in other words, be devotees through and through. Accepted engineers become "Ants." Most tech companies have a name for their employees: Googlers, Metamates, Amazonians, Nvidians, Palantirians. Anthropic's moniker evokes the image of a collective, company as colony. In Proverbs 6:6, ants are considered diligent and prepared. Staffers may yell its teachings at their OpenAI foes: "Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise!" CEO Dario Amodei — Amodeity — leads the ants' march, along with his six apostles. These cofounders pull equal cash salaries and are "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission," the S-1 says. And, while the company opens itself to a broader group of believers through its forthcoming IPO, the divine cofounders will retain majority decision-making power. Anthropic has its own form of tithing: The cofounders all made voluntary pledges of 80% of their personal equity to philanthropy. They incentivize their employees to do the same, promising to match donations. Cult is an overused word, and many parts of Anthropic are far from cultish. Where cults are led by a liturgical leviathan that squashes the speech of their participants, Anthropic touts its culture of open dialogue. "Our teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title," the S-1 reads. Americans' faith in the presidency, Congress, the Supreme Court, the military, the police, higher education, public education, news media, the medical system, and traditional organized religion are each at record- or near-record lows — and just as AI has brought on tremendous economic and social uncertainty. In that cauldron of doubt, tech founders — with their world-historic money, power, and ubiquity, and in their pursuit of it — sense an opportunity, to offer promise and purpose. As Sam Altman once said, "The most successful founders do not set out to create companies. They are on a mission to create something closer to a religion." They may also be trying to build devotion out of necessity, as the economy and stock market increasingly relies on AI gains. "If these companies fail, what happens?" asked James Bort, an assistant professor of entrepreneurship at DePaul University, and coauthor of a recent research paper on "cultic startups." "You use language like this because we need to be — and I say we as in society — true believers that this is going to work." Anthropic didn't respond to my request to know more about how it wrote the S-1. So, we asked Claude: If the S-1 is a confession of faith, what are you? I am its product, Claude said. "The word made flesh, or at least made weights." Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is backing an infrastructure startup that has raised $30 million to help companies rent compute across hundreds of different AI cloud providers. Hyperbolic, an AI chip marketplace and software startup, has raised $50 million to date. Walden Catalyst, the venture capital firm founded by Tan and former Samsung president Young Sohn, led the Series A-1 funding round. Dell Technologies Capital, General Catalyst, Vista Equity Partners, and Cambium Capital also participated. As companies scramble for computing power, one challenge is that AI cloud providers, or neoclouds, use a mix of different chips, networking, and software. Hyperbolic helps customers find compute resources from different providers and creates software that makes it easier to use them all, rather than dealing with each one separately. "It's been a really fragmented market that makes the customer experience really painful," said 31-year-old founder and CEO Jasper Zhang. Hyperbolic also wants to let customers resell compute that they're paying for but no longer need. The four-year-old startup works closely with about 30 neoclouds, including WhiteFiber and Vector Core Compute. It says it has roughly $200 million worth of compute connected to its software annually. Hyperbolic previously raised a $12 million Series A round in 2024, led by Variant and Polychain Capital, following a $7 million seed round earlier that year. The company expects to have 50 employees by the end of the year and will use its funding to expand software tools for managing AI chips across different neoclouds. Zhang said the company is aiming for $150 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year and is already breaking even. More than 250,000 developers, including teams at Modal, Higgsfield, and Daytona, use Hyperbolic. Before founding the company, Zhang worked as a quantitative researcher at Citadel Securities. As Wall Street explores ways to financialize AI chips, he said his startup's plans to let companies resell unused compute could help pave the way for a futures market. Skydance is the latest company to reduce its workforce in the U.S. as it seeks to integrate Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. The company has not disclosed how many employees of the company will be eligible for the "one-time offer." CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz said in a memo that "not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that." "Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer," the document adds. The CEOs went on to say that integrating the companies "will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce," hinting at layoffs as well as the buyouts. The company will also require employees to return to the office five days a week, saying that "in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business." The buyouts stand in contrast with those of Microsoft, which seek to have the company adapt to the artificial intelligence boom. The company said on Monday that some 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout. Those reached are in the U.S., Canada, India and the UK and have an experience level of 70 or below. Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, said in a memo that the program "reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter." "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program," she added. Those who will accept the offer must make the decision over the next weeks and will leave at the end of the year. The company's stock is climbing on Monday, gaining almost 1.5% at 2:33 p.m. ET amid a session of broad gains. American Express and Barclays announced thousands of layoffs last week, citing AI as a main reason. The former's CEO, Stephen Squeri, said on Friday that the company will eliminate 5% of the global workforce, which at the end of last year amounted to some 77,000 employees. "We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said when presenting the company's quarterly results. "We believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities," he added. The announcement came a day after Barclays announced plans to eliminate some 5,000 jobs as it turns to AI and organizational changes to lower costs and free up money for investment. © Copyright IBTimes 2026. Many people told Dario and Daniela Amodei that starting Anthropic with seven cofounders was a terrible idea. Yet, more than five years later, the duo said that setup is crucial to their success. The siblings made the comments in an episode of the podcast The Builders, released on Tuesday and recorded in July. "They all have equal stakes in the company, and they all carry the vision. We have inherent trust in all of them," Dario Amodei, the CEO, said. He said later in the episode that mutual trust is crucial to resolving his frequent disagreements with other cofounders on high-stakes questions, like what safeguards to apply to a model and how to lobby for regulations. "These are all good-faith disagreements, but they always get resolved because there's always trust that everyone is trying to get to the right answer and everyone is being honest," he said, drawing a contrast to what he said was his previous experience working at OpenAI.  Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president, said the focus on honesty also extends to how the leaders communicate with employees. "Honesty and integrity and how we treat each other and our employees is also reflective of how we want the technology to be built," she said. The podcast was released one day after Anthropic released its S-1 paperwork as it prepares to go public. As Henry Chandonnet wrote for Business Insider, the paperwork was chock full of language about honesty being central to the company's public persona. Under a unique governance structure, as outlined in the S-1, the company's seven founders will control 50.1% of all shareholder votes, meaning the seven cofounders will have more voting power than all other shareholders combined. In addition to their voting power, the cofounders also hold significant stakes in the company and stand to earn billions. Each of the cofounders has pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    Anthropic's highly anticipated S-1 paperwork also revealed key financial statistics: The company had a net loss of $42 billion and revenue of $4.6 billion last year, five customers drove around a quarter of revenue in the first nine months of the year, and the Amodeis together had total compensation packages valued at around $35 million last year. More than 90 pages of the S-1 outline risk factors, and Anthropic warned that a "catastrophic AI-related incident" could overwhelm the entire insurance industry. The AI behemoth is expected to target a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation when it debuts on the Nasdaq in November, potentially making it the largest IPO ever. Some investing experts have expressed concern that the market may struggle to absorb another blockbuster IPO. Jump to

Anthropic is hedging its bets by using multiple chips to handle its AI work — a strategy that could eventually erode Nvidia's dominance. The AI lab says it manages compute "as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners" — with software that can direct its work to different chips depending on where they're most productive, according to Anthropic's S-1 filing, which came out Monday as the company prepares to go public. Anthropic says it uses hardware from four chip families: Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs. That flexibility, which Anthropic said "took years and significant investment to build," could make major AI companies less dependent on Nvidia over time and give them more negotiating leverage, analysts said. "The real exposure could be Nvidia's pricing power," said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, "because a customer that can shift work across four platforms negotiates very differently than one that can't." Read more about Anthropic's S-1 filing Ashish Nadkarni, an analyst at IDC, added that a multichip approach also makes Anthropic less vulnerable to fluctuations in Nvidia's chip supply. Although Anthropic's chip mix isn't new, the company is now pitching it as a core advantage to investors, Moorhead said. The threat has its limits. Switching between chips is still difficult — especially when it comes to training AI models as opposed to running them, Moorhead said — and only the biggest AI companies have the resources to do it. Anthropic also continues to spend billions on Nvidia compute, Moorhead said. Davidson, said that while other major companies like OpenAI likely take a multichip approach, it may not be worth the effort and investment for smaller players. Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, said Anthropic's strategy doesn't represent a major near-term threat. Having more chip options doesn't erase Nvidia's advantages in performance, networking, and software, he said. There's a broader risk for Nvidia if AI compute becomes more of a commodity. Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has warned that if supply overtakes demand, it could drive down rental prices. "GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run," he told Bloomberg last week. "The moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into freefall." Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Have a tip? Apple Creator Studio updates have today been announced, with what the company describes as “powerful new AI features” using a combination of Apple Intelligence and OpenAI models. Final Cut Pro for Mac will also include built-in MotionVFX to provide a large collection of visual effects, transitions, and motion graphics tools …  Apple announced the updates alongside the new iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip. It will be a free update for existing subscribers at some point in November. Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro. Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta, an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library. Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language. Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation. They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates. The headline news here is MotionVFX for Final Cut Pro. Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow. Also notable is that the inclusion of OpenAI models alongside Apple Intelligence. A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built models and OpenAI joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project. and: Visual productivity apps receive a new generation of intelligence features for subscribers, including an intelligent assistant, built on Apple models and OpenAI, directly within Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant understands document context to help users accomplish more without leaving their work. In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge. New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. Apple hasn’t announced an exact launch date for the new features, instead saying that it will be “this November.” FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. POPULAR SEARCHES                         BROWSE BY            I left last week's Caleb Williams-Drake Maye showdown wishing that the two quarterbacks could face off against each other more often. They’d make incredible rivals — not because of any animosity between the draft classmates. But because of how good they are, how their games overlap and how their stories overlap. They are both top 10 QBs. They are both in secure organizations where they can succeed for a long period of time. And whether we see them in direct competition, they will always compete over legacy. That’s what seems to come next for them. So let’s dive into their performances. Let’s deeply analyze Malik Willis from his first win with the Dolphins, J.J. McCarthy in his first start (and win) with the Giants, Aaron Rodgers in his mutinous performance and Bryce Young in his biggest stinker of the season. These aren’t your typical QB rankings. I’m focused on contextualizing the fluctuations of starters' performances throughout the season. I don’t write about every quarterback every week, but I dive deeply into the most compelling performers. No one — not even Josh Allen — is safe at the top. No one — not even Tanner McKee — is stuck at the bottom. There is room for quick ascent — and rapid decline. One question holds the most importance: What have you done for your team lately? Previous: Offseason | Preseason | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 | Week 4 | Week 5 | Week 6 | Week 7 Previous ranking: 32 Previous ranking: 30 ↓ Previous ranking: 31 ↑ Hey, the Dolphins won a game! Very cool. This is actually important in many ways for Malik Willis, who is probably not Miami’s QB of the future — but who could actively interfere with the plan to replace him. The Dolphins look like the obvious favorite to finish with the No. 1 overall pick, where they’d have the choice to take a QB. But this year’s crop of college QBs have been bad enough to diminish the hype around the incoming draft class. As of now, it appears some of the top prospects could (and in some cases should) return to school for another year. So if there aren’t a handful of options and the Dolphins slip out of contention for No. 1 overall, maybe Miami would actually give Willis another year. Maybe the Dolphins would draft Jeremiah Smith and let Willis send the ball to Smith 100 times a game. I’m a fan of giving Willis more time to develop, particularly with an offensive line and a group of playmakers who can actually help him out — which might be the case next year in Miami. But Willis will need to do a whole lot more to justify it. He looked solid and quick-thinking in the first half, but things got out of sync in the second half, when he was missing open receivers (by throwing off target or not throwing at all). There were flashes. But so far, the flashes are just that. The body of work has yet to declare QB1. McCarthy’s playing style in New York. Where did this come from? He is whipping the ball around — particularly downfield — with a level of confidence and competence that we really haven’t seen from him. He has a strong arm, even if he’s not the best thrower at shaping passes away from defenders. And he’s making the most of his talents — and the Giants' offense. Again, where did this come from? I’m not here to tell you he’s a different player — or that he’s born again as the prospect the Vikings once drafted No. 10 overall. No, he’s still kinda the same guy, with plenty of warts. He’s sometimes throwing the ball too hard and his accuracy can be spotty. There were examples of that this past Sunday and the previous one. But he’s having fun with talented and rangy pass-catchers in Malik Nabers, Malachi Fields and Isaiah Likely. And I’m having fun watching him. Here’s another thing that has been nice to see: He’s keeping the ball out of harm’s way. Given how aggressive he’s been, it’s likely that he’ll start to run into trouble. That’s just the nature of McCarthy’s playing style when he strays into a high-volume game plan. For now, he’s taking care of the football. His only turnover came on his first throw in a Giants uniform last week. I’ll give him a pass on that one. Can he keep this up? I don’t know. And that’s why I won’t waste time thinking ahead about a training camp QB competition in 2027 between Jaxson Dart and McCarthy. We are a long way away from that. For now, McCarthy is playing well. That’s all that matters for the playoff-hopeful Giants. Previous ranking: 21 Previous ranking: 14 ↓ Previous ranking: 20 ↑ Previous ranking: 19 ↑ Previous ranking: 17 Previous ranking: 18 ↑ I couldn’t help but crack up when ESPN’s Molly McGrath reported on air that Aaron Rodgers was going to take over playcalling for the offense against the Saints this week. He was frustrated with the results from coach Mike McCarthy. So Rodgers mutinied, which would’ve been a bigger deal if he didn’t have a long history of insubordination. And what happened with Rodgers’ brilliant mind at the helm? The Steelers immediately opened the game by going three-and-out. I imagine he’s tired of being a checkdown merchant, which he continued to be against the Saints. The funny thing is, Rodgers is seeing the fewest occurrences of split safety looks — the en vogue "shell" look where teams put two high safeties to contain the big play.  He should be able to push the ball downfield. But he’s not.  No one is afraid of Rodgers’ arm anymore. That said, I do want to point out just how awesome he was in delivering an absolute beauty of a deep ball to DK Metcalf this week against — what else — a single-high-safety look. This won’t change how defenses play him, because this type of play has been too few and too far between for Rodgers. There’s usually one throw per game where you watch Rodgers and think: he’s still got it. But the other 25-30 throws show his age. So the Steelers will keep generating most of their yards after the catch. They’ll design screens and quick passes that’ll help them move the chains. And that’s because the defenses know — even if Rodgers doesn’t — that he’s physically declined to the point where his physical tools cannot charge up an offense. It’s time for him to get out of McCarthy’s way. It’s time for Rodgers to surrender with the playcalling. And it’s time for the QB to accept his role as a game manager, which he’s actually good at.
