Janus Henderson, a London-based asset manager overseeing roughly $500 billion, is bringing one of Wall Street’s best-known stock indexes onto blockchain rails through an issuer-sponsored fund. The launch comes amid an escalating debate over who gets to tokenize traditional securities. The firm teamed up with tokenization platform Centrifuge to launch JQQQ, a fund tracking the Nasdaq-100 Index, home to tech giants including Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft. The fund is issued on the Stellar XLM$0.1853 blockchain, the companies said Tuesday. JQQQ follows the introduction of a similar onchain index fund product last year, the Janus Henderson Anemoy S&P 500 Fund (SPXA), which was the first tokenized index fund licensed by the S&P Dow Jones Indices. Janus Henderson said its onchain investment platform now includes more than $1 billion across Treasuries, structured credit and equities. The launch marks another step in Wall Street’s push to bring traditional investments onchain, expanding beyond U.S. Treasuries, money market funds and private credit into stock-market products. It also highlights a growing divide between funds issued onchain by their managers and third-party tokens created without the underlying companies’ involvement. JQQQ follows the issuer-sponsored model. Janus Henderson issues and manages the fund, Centrifuge provides the blockchain infrastructure and Nasdaq licenses the index to track. That differs from third-party stock tokens, which may be backed by shares held in custody or structured as separate instruments tracking stock prices. Investors in those products don't necessarily own the underlying shares or receive shareholder rights. The distinction has become central in the debate around tokenization efforts. Most recently, 22 companies objected to plans for blockchain-based trading of their shares on the OKX-ICE venue, adding to a debate over whether issuers should have a say when their stocks are tokenized. “As investors explore new ways to access markets through digital infrastructure, demand continues to grow for exposure to established, transparent benchmarks,” said Sean Wasserman, head of index product management at Nasdaq. The fund also shows how tokenization is moving beyond digital versions of existing investments toward products built to operate on blockchains from the start. Such funds could eventually allow investors to use their holdings as collateral for loans or move them between blockchain-based financial applications, subject to regulatory requirements and platform support. "Tokenization becomes much more powerful when the assets investors want to own can also become building blocks for an onchain financial system," said Anil Sood, chief strategy and growth officer at Centrifuge. Drone hit a market in the city that serves as the de facto capital of the paramilitary RSF in Darfur, resident says. Save Share A drone strike in Nyala, in Sudan’s Darfur region, has killed at least 21 people and injured 40 others, the AFP news agency reported, citing a medical source and witnesses. A Nyala resident said the attack took place at about 8pm (18:00 GMT) on Monday at a market in the north of the city, which serves as the de facto capital of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). “Twenty-one people were killed in last night’s bombing, and more than 40 others injured,” a medic at Nyala Hospital said on Tuesday. Another Nyala resident told AFP that the market was frequented by armed men, particularly RSF fighters. The Sudanese military, which has been at war with the RSF since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivalling the military-backed, internationally recognised government in Khartoum. The attack comes as the warring sides are increasingly turning to drone warfare. Earlier this month, the RSF launched strikes targeting Khartoum’s airport, as well as dams and power stations in the government-controlled east. An RSF drone attack on Tuesday “targeted the al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting power supplies for millions across large parts of Khartoum and Gezira state”, a national electricity company told AFP on condition of anonymity. It followed Monday’s coordinated RSF drone strikes on six power stations, which cut off electricity to millions in the states of Gezira, White Nile, Sennar and Gadarif. A government drone attack in a disputed border region between Sudan and South Sudan earlier this month killed more than 150 people. The war began in 2023 when a dispute over how to integrate the two forces erupted into clashes in the capital, Khartoum. The fighting has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 13 million, and created the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises. On Monday, the United States, the European Union and 30 other countries warned of an “alarming deterioration” in food access in Sudan and called for “urgent action” to prevent famine. In a joint statement released by the US State Department on Monday, the signatories called on the groups fighting Sudan’s civil war “to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance”. Join this webinar to choose a channel to test, set a starting budget, and identify results to track before investing more. Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source. This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data. Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo. Your traffic is flat, and you don’t have a budget to throw at the problem. What should you test first? And how do you get your boss to approve an experiment when you can’t promise it will work? I put those questions to Jonathan Berthold, VP of Revenue at Ziff Davis, on The Search Engine Journal podcast. Jonathan is a longtime marketing strategist who works in both SEO and paid media. We covered where to find bottom-of-funnel opportunities and how to keep a test small enough that it can’t take down a site. We also discussed how long to wait before judging a result, along with a gap he sees in both SEO and paid media: Marketers focus on generating traffic and overlook what happens after a user lands on the site.  [00:45] What To Test When Traffic Is Flat And Budget Is Tight [02:44] Getting Leadership Buy-In For Experiments [06:35] Testing Small Before Making Sitewide Changes [07:37] How Long To Run An SEO Experiment [09:00] How To Evaluate Paid Media Tests [10:51] Landing Page And Funnel Tests Marketers Overlook [13:04] Finding Link Opportunities In AI Citation Data [14:29] Why Search Intent Matters More Than Volume When traffic is flat and there’s no budget, Jonathan starts with a full site analysis to find out why traffic stalled. He has inherited sites in that condition before, ranging from B2C SaaS companies to informational lead-generation sites. What he finds in the analysis determines the fix. Sometimes that means improving existing pages, and sometimes it means building new pages to fill a topic gap. Either way, his experiment would target commercial intent. Top-of-funnel traffic is being “siphoned by LLMs, AI Overviews, AI Mode,” he said, and that traffic “is going away and/or doesn’t really convert or add to the bottom line.” So he would test one of two approaches: optimizing existing pages for commercial and transactional keywords, or creating new content to fill topic gaps in the market. Without a budget, Jonathan relies on AI to do the research. He uses it to learn what type of content ranks for bottom-of-funnel terms and where the opportunities are to scale traffic in areas competitors aren’t covering. He also uses it to figure out what added perspective would make the new pages “unique and inviting to search engines like Google.” I asked what test most marketers should be running but aren’t. Jonathan said there is “a massive market for bottom-of-funnel traffic that a lot of SEOs sleep on.” It’s easier to build a strategy around keywords with more than a thousand monthly searches, but many of those keywords are informational. Giants like Reddit, LinkedIn and Wikipedia already rank for them, and LLMs, AI Overviews and AI Mode have absorbed much of that traffic. He called bottom-of-funnel targeting “100% the easiest low lift opportunity” available. Jonathan sees approval as a communication problem. He never tells a leader that the team will test something and hope for a result. Every experiment is an opportunity to learn. He starts with a hypothesis, and the pitch explains what the test will reveal. It might show whether a tactic or process will help in the future, or whether a messaging or creative idea holds up. He recommends framing the ask around the long-term payoff by explaining what the team will learn and how that knowledge will make it better at its craft. When the pitch is positioned as “this experiment will allow us to learn X, Y, and Z so that we can earn this much into the future,” he said, it is “easier understood by a leadership team that largely works within P&L.” I raised a concern about the quick fixes circulating now that newcomers are using to enter SEO through AEO and GEO. Those tactics work until the algorithm catches up. I’d rather keep experiments contained than put an entire website at risk. Jonathan agrees. When a team runs an SEO test across a full website and the test goes in the wrong direction, “you tank the whole organic,” he said. His rule for both SEO and paid media is to start with a very small section, then iterate and expand slowly as the results come in. Paid media taught him the same lesson. Tripling a budget in one day “ruins all the optimization,” he said, so budgets need to rise gradually each day while the system learns. In SEO, the equivalent mistake is rolling out a schema or content-writing experiment sitewide and tanking pages that already perform well. Results also need to be replicated. A result should repeat “so that it’s not just a random result,” he said, until a pattern emerges that you can apply to the rest of your work. When a test isn’t going the way you hoped, when should you stop? Years ago, the standard advice was to give an SEO test six to nine months, especially for a new site, but iterations move much faster now. I asked Jonathan how he decides whether to give a struggling experiment more time or end it. For SEO, he gives an experiment about a month. He relies on Search Console and treats its data as directional. Google needs time to crawl the updated pages, process the changes and adjust rankings before impressions and clicks move, so “definitely within a week, you won’t see results.” After 30 days, there is usually enough data to see whether impressions are moving, and he would wait 60 days at most. He said starting small helps here, too, because it keeps expectations in check and lets the rest of the team’s work continue while the experiment runs. Paid media follows a different rule because the feedback is immediate. He either reviews tests every two weeks or uses his preferred method, which is a spend threshold of two to three times the target cost per acquisition. Once a test has spent that much, it has run its course, and the team can either iterate on it or kill it. Jonathan sees the same gap in SEO and paid media. Marketers put nearly all their attention on generating traffic and overlook “what happens when a user actually hits your website.” Any page that already draws a lot of organic traffic, or that a team spends heavily to send paid traffic to, is a good candidate for split testing and funnel optimization. Landing page and funnel experiments should always be “an on thing,” he said, because you can keep raising conversion rates at each stage of the funnel, “even by a few basis percentage points.” Jonathan is also running his own experiment that connects bottom-of-funnel targeting with link building. He uses AI citation data “to unearth link building opportunities.” He sees it as a way to spot where LLMs are heading and to build brand presence by earning the citations competitors have. Many companies stop short of that step. A lot of them track AI visibility and watch which sites cite their competitors, he said, “but not a lot are taking the next step, which is reaching out to these publications.” The payoff compounds. Pages that cite competitors for bottom-of-funnel keywords likely rank for those keywords themselves and get cited often in LLMs. Earning a mention on those pages can send traffic to your site and get your brand cited alongside your competitors, which he called “a more holistic approach.” Jonathan no longer puts much stock in search volume. Search habits change every day. If the context and topic are right, a long-tail keyword can still be worth targeting even when Google, Moz or another platform reports it at one, 10 or zero searches a month. Volume is useful as a directional signal, especially in paid media, where it helps set expectations for the total addressable market. In organic search, fragmentation changes the math. People search in more ways than they used to, including inside LLMs, and LLMs run their own query fan-outs. That makes targeting “how your target ICP searches” more important than the number in a keyword tool. His example comes from his agency days. A client in the composites industry supplied fiberglass conduits for commercial projects. Its total addressable market was very small, and its keywords had very low search volume. But if 10 people searched a month and two of them landed on the site, “very likely they’re in that market. That’s a half-a-million-dollar contract.” That’s where conversion rate comes in. Someone searching for the best mortgage rates will likely end up on informational content and probably won’t convert on that site. A search like “I need a plumber to fix my toilet” may show little search volume, but the person typing it has an urgent need and high intent, so they are much more likely to convert. As LLMs become more widely used, he expects search volume to be “not fully representative” of the phrases people use or the many fan-out queries a single keyword can generate. As AI answers absorb informational searches, Jonathan says focus on high-intent searches, even when the volume is low. He also recommends running tests on the pages where visitors decide whether to convert. A small test in those places can show a measurable business result within a month or two. That result also makes the next experiment easier to get approved. A test tied to conversions produces a number that a leadership team can use to make sound decisions. Rodney Carmichael                        SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Jay-Z looks on prior to the start of Super Bowl LX  between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California.                                                           Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images                                       hide caption  It's no small irony that Jay-Z, the best personification of hip-hop's hopes and dreams, built his success by emulating America's worst excesses. Avarice. Greed. Domination. In turn, we idolized him for showing us "how to move in a room full of vultures." The streets he hustled in were made savage by design. The industry he conquered was out to vanquish him first. Indoctrinated by the same vampiric systems, we learned to praise those willing to sacrifice humanity — whether theirs or others' — in order to scale from the bottom up. The oppressor-oppressed dialectic can be funny that way. If you're not careful, you start to become the monster you're running from. According to an announcement from the NFL, Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show in February. He's reached a new pinnacle. Not the first rapper to play the halftime show, but the first act with the power to plug himself into that highly coveted slot. The gig even came with a $25 million paycheck, if you count the 2019 deal his entertainment agency Roc Nation scored to book the NFL's annual Super Bowl lineup. The game is to be sold, as the saying goes. And this time, a true player got to set the rules of engagement. After seven years of curating the talent — and pushing rap to the forefront in unprecedented fashion — he's poised to stick the proverbial feather in his Yankees fitted. Yet, hip-hop's response has been ambivalent. Some of us don't know whether we want to slow clap or slapbox with the god. Whether it's viewed as a crowning achievement or the culmination of a deal that made Jigga the perfect "Black face" to whitewash the NFL's sullied image — per Colin Kaepernick's recent recounting (comments Jay-Z has not responded to) — ultimately depends on which version of the story hip-hop's most valuable hustler can convincingly sell. Like water to a whale. Fresh off a PR crisis himself, Jay-Z's been engaged in his own rebranding campaign this year. It follows the recently recanted rape allegations made in a civil lawsuit that named Jay-Z and Sean "Diddy" Combs as co-defendants. (Jay-Z vehemently denied the allegations from the start and pursued a defamation and extortion lawsuit against the filing attorney, Tony Buzbee, which was also recently dismissed by an appellate court. Combs also denied the allegations against him and was sentenced to more than four years in prison on prostitution-related charges.) Surviving such a public smear campaign lent new meaning to the 30th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt. "We played enough defense, 2026 is all offense," as he told GQ's senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe in March. So he brought back the umlauts over his chosen name. He sheared off the Basquiat locs grown for both his daughter, Blue Ivy, and his deceased uncle. And he sold out Yankee Stadium three nights in a row. But he's nobody's sellout. That was the underlying message of his anti-protest freestyle on night one. With smug confidence, he responded to the backlash for making his vinyl reissue available exclusively at Target in the middle of a grassroots Black boycott to combat the retailer's DEI policy reversal. "They say I sold out. Yeah, I did sell out. Three nights. I sold Yankee Stadium the hell out," he rapped a capella as a prelude to "Politics As Usual." There's this erroneous idea that Jay-Z's image rehab is oddly out of character. It's bolstered by the belief that he's always been oblivious to what the general public thinks. He can afford to be. But the truth is he's always been keenly aware and blatantly responsive to critique — whether cultural or personal in nature. When he likened himself to "Che Guevara with bling on / I'm complex" on "Public Service Announcement (Interlude)," it was in direct response to former Village Voice and Vibe journalist Elizabeth Méndez Berry, who provoked him to consider the contradictions he laid bare by donning a diamond-encrusted Jesus piece atop a t-shirt featuring the Cuban revolutionary's face. "The piece was smacking Che Guevara upside the head," Méndez Berry recently told The Ringer's Joel Anderson. "Communism and capitalism colliding with every step." When Harry Belafonte called out Jay and Beyoncé by name in 2012 and 2013 to criticize Black celebrities for "turn[ing] their back on social responsibility," Jay clapped back. "My presence is charity," he said in an interview with hip-hop journalist Elliott Wilson. His response also showed up in criminal justice reforms he pushed to address disproportionate rates of incarceration in the Black community. Even Decoded, his 2010 book written with dream hampton, was a first-person explainer meant to contextualize his lyrics with the liner notes of his lived experience. His latest explanatory foray, the eight-episode HBO documentary Jay-Z in 8, pairs him with former Def Jam founder and producer/guru Rick Rubin. Appropriately set in the austere environs of France's former stock exchange, they sit across from one another for deep listening sessions of Jay's discography meant to trigger revelations. He covers the Che Guevara moment again. He talks about what it meant to confront his dad — who abandoned the family when Jay was 11 — just one month before his death. They talk generational trauma and family secrets. He even fills in some unredacted details from his hustling era. Mostly, he tics and bobs his head to the beat like rap's Rainman, shuffling through stored volumes of lyrics famously composed and committed to memory without ever having touched a pen. No one does this dance between dualities better. Encoding performances for those who lived it. Translating rhymes for those consuming from a privileged distance. This Duboisian double consciousness is what makes him such an articulate marketer of the American Dream, a propaganda artist for Black excellence and capitalist exploits. For Jay, crossing over didn't come through rapping. It came through his extracurricular moves. The brand sponsorships. The lucrative partnerships. Essentially, he became a cultural broker. The gatekeeper handing the key for entry over to the highest bidder. He played a key role in unlocking the Nets-NBA deal for developer Bruce Ratner that made Barclays Center the catalyst for gentrifying Brooklyn. Jay gained a minority ownership stake (.067 percent); longtime Brooklynites got displaced. He gave cover for Roger Goodell and the NFL to sidestep Colin Kaepernick's protests on behalf of Black America. The league's billionaire owners got a pass; racial injustice got performative slogans and empty charitable initiatives. "Over and over, Jay is the one that powerful whites use to quiet Negro protests so they can make more money together," former hip-hop journalist Touré recently said, likening Jay-Z to a house Negro who repeatedly aligns himself with the white power structure while claiming to represent Black folks' come-up. The same conclusion is drawn by prominent video essayist F.D Signifier, who categorizes Jay-Z as part of the "Black misleadership class." But the biggest condemnation actually comes from Jigga himself. In the final episode of Jay-Z in 8 — the documentary he co-executive produced — Jay also calls out so-called race hustlers and house Negroes who act as "extortionists" that "go to one place and say: You want our support? Give us the money." It's as if he doesn't realize how much his own actions resemble the behavior he's side-eyeing. "We['re] not getting it as a race together," he says. "We're slowly getting there separately, but it's not a concerted effort of us to align our powers and our finances to benefit our community." We could blame Jay, but as he once rapped on "P.S.A.," he didn't invent the game. He "just rolled the dice, trying to get some change." When he hits that Super Bowl halftime stage at SoFi Stadium next year, he'll be playing with a pocketful of house money. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. THE LATEST TRENDS IN MODERN HOUSE DESIGN AND DECORATING Country farmhouse decor is one of those styles that actually gets more comfortable the longer you live with it. The pieces don’t try too hard, the colors don’t fight you, and the whole thing somehow looks better after a few years of real use. These 8 country farmhouse decor ideas show you exactly what to borrow. Table of Contents Country farmhouse works because it isn’t precious. It leans on real wood, soft fabrics, and colors that come from a garden instead of a trend report, which is why these rooms still look good ten years in. The style forgives a kid, a dog, and a cup of coffee that didn’t make it to the coaster. What follows is a mix of living spaces, entryways, and a couple of harder-working rooms where the farmhouse look stops being just pretty and starts earning its keep. Each one gives you a different piece of the puzzle you can actually copy at home. Sage green walls do all the heavy lifting here because the color reads neutral to the eye but still gives the room a mood. Pair it with warm wood beams and a cream couch and the whole space feels like it’s been sitting there for decades. If you want this look, pick a green with gray in it, not yellow, so it stays calm against stone and natural light. Our living room interiors edit has more rooms built around this exact kind of palette. A long open shelf, a row of iron hooks, and a bench with baskets underneath turns any blank wall into a functional entry. The whitewashed shiplap, those flat horizontal boards you see in farmhouse rooms, keeps it bright instead of heavy. What makes it work is the mix of storage styles: open shelves for the stuff you want to see, baskets for the stuff you don’t. Worth bookmarking if you’re reworking a small foyer. That dining table is the whole point of this room. The thick reclaimed planks have cracks, dark grain, and metal brackets that look like they belonged to something else first, which is the whole appeal. Mix tufted upholstered chairs with a plain white Windsor and the table stops looking like it needs matching furniture to feel finished. A piece this honest is worth hunting down secondhand instead of buying new. Most farmhouse rooms stay low and cozy, but this one goes the other way: huge vaulted ceiling, exposed trusses, and a wrought iron chandelier big enough to anchor the whole floor. The furniture stays simple on purpose so your eye keeps traveling up. If you’ve got the ceiling height, don’t fight it with small light fixtures, go bigger than you think you need. Farmhouse homes go deeper into this kind of layout. Here’s where country farmhouse meets a little bohemian: warm wood ceiling, white shiplap walls, and a chunky macrame chandelier that keeps the space from feeling too serious. The gray sectional and tribal rug ground the lighter textures above, so nothing feels like it’s floating. This is a good move if you like farmhouse bones but don’t want everything to look like a magazine shoot from 2015. Rough plank ceilings, a split-log mantel, and two old Windsor chairs flanking the hearth, this is country farmhouse at its most honest. The persian rug underneath pulls in the only real color, and the slipcovered couch keeps everything else neutral so the texture of the wood gets to be the star. If your room doesn’t have the architectural bones, a reclaimed wood beam over the fireplace fakes the rest. Fireplace interiors has more rooms built around this move. Reclaimed wood walls, a stone countertop with raw edges, and two vessel sinks that look like river rocks turn an ordinary double vanity into something worth looking at. The oil-rubbed bronze faucets and small shaded sconces are what tie the whole thing to the farmhouse side instead of pure cabin. Keep the floor in slate or stone to carry the mood all the way down. Olive green cabinets paired with warm brick and a butcher-block island is the country kitchen a lot of people are quietly moving toward right now. White kitchens aren’t going anywhere, but this is the version that feels like a real family cooks here. The gold candelabra chandeliers are the one fancy move in a room full of practical materials, and they’re what keeps it from looking like a farmhouse cliche. The rest of the kitchen interiors edit goes further into warm-toned cabinet colors. Republicans are feeling the high-cost crunch. The latest consumer sentiment reading out of the University of Michigan finds that, across the board, Americans are still feeling bad. While self-identified Republicans still feel better than their Democratic and Independent counterparts, they're increasingly feeling the pinch of rising prices. From January to October 2026, the share of Republicans citing high prices as a drag on their finances rose the most out of all political factions. It's a sign that, even as their party holds Congress and the White House, Republican voters might still be feeling the heat — especially as inflation continues to rise. And, more broadly, Republicans seem to be souring on economic conditions. A Pew Research survey of 5,062 American adults from September 28 to October 4 found that Republicans, and those who lean Republican, were becoming less likely to say that economic conditions in the country are good. Historically, consumer sentiment and surveys asking voters about economic conditions tend to have strong partisan correlations. Democrats are more likely to say that the economy is doing well and they're optimistic about the future when a Democrat is president; Republicans do the same when the GOP holds the White House. Do you have thoughts on high prices or inflation? Contact this reporter at jkaplan@businessinsider.com. The shift in Republican sentiment illustrates just how bad Americans at large are feeling about the economy. A similar downshift happened among Democrats amid the inflationary spike during President Joe Biden's term. "President Trump has implemented an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda that has blunted Biden's historic 40-year high inflation crisis, driven economic growth, increased wages and created private-sector jobs in areas that had been hollowed out and shipped overseas," White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in a statement. "The President has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but this administration will continue to deliver economic wins for the American people over the next two years." While 18% of Republicans surveyed by Pew in January 2026 said that President Donald Trump's economic policies have made economic conditions worse, that share grew to 35% in October 2026. Similarly, an increasing share — 14% in January versus 25% in October — said that they expect economic conditions to be worse a year from now. Similarly, polling from SSRS's Economic Attitudes Tracker found that Republicans are now more likely to describe the economy as bad than good — and the share of Independents who think the economy is good has plummeted to 12%, compared to a high of 25% in August 2025.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    The cost concerns come as Iran War volatility — and the resulting fallout on energy prices — kept inflation high. In September, the consumer price index accelerated more than anticipated, with skyrocketing energy prices driving the increase. That means that, for the sixth month in a row, inflation has outpaced wage increases. Meanwhile, the labor market is floundering, with the country adding a paltry 29,000 payrolls in September — a far cry from the 90,000 roles economists predicted. Midterm Election Day is a week away, and partisan sentiment around prices is shaping up to be especially important at the ballot box. Affordability messaging has become a touchpoint in swing state elections, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle clamoring to show how their policies have and will bring down everyday costs. But the declining sentiment among even the Republican base could be a warning sign for conservatives: An Ipsos/Washington Post/ABC News poll found that, in April, 34% of respondents said they trusted Republicans to do a better job of handling the economy, compared to 33% saying the same of Democrats. IBM, Oracle, Intel and IonQ have opted out of plans by crypto exchange OKX and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) to offer blockchain-based trading of their shares, bringing the total number of issuer objections to 26. The four companies were named in an updated public notice dated Monday, Oct. 26, from OKXICE, the two firms’ joint venture. They join earlier objectors including Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Cisco and Wells Fargo. The growing list underscores a hurdle for OKXICE and the SEC’s new framework for tokenized stock trading: building a market that issuers are willing to join. The agency’s five-year “Innovation Exemption” gives qualifying venues room to test round-the-clock blockchain-based trading of stocks, and it also gives public companies an option to block their shares from being offered. OKXICE issued its initial public notice on Oct. 4, outlining plans to use Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, with transactions settled in stablecoins. The venue would use automated market makers — software that executes trades through pools of assets rather than matching buyers and sellers through a conventional order book. Under the framework, venues must notify issuers and give them 30 days to object before offering tokenized versions of their shares. All four newly disclosed objectors were among the 62 companies in OKXICE’s original proposed roster. That brings objections from the original selection to 23, or about 37%, according to a CoinDesk tally. The overall count also includes Cerebras Systems, Arm Holdings and Wells Fargo, which were absent from that from the original selection. The growing list of objections highlights early issuer caution about plans to trade their shares under the SEC’s new framework. The rules give companies a say in how their shares come onchain, but also tilts the decision toward opting out, industry experts told CoinDesk’s Tokenization Weekly. Objecting costs nothing, while staying silent allows trading to begin without a mechanism to withdraw that consent later. For legal and investor-relations teams still getting familiar with the arrangements, saying no leaves more time to understand them. The financial benefit for issuers is also uncertain yet. Tokenization could bring additional demand, particularly from overseas investors, but that may not be enough to offset concerns about thin, round-the-clock trading outside the familiar market structure, TD Securities’ Reid Noch previously told CoinDesk. Andrew Cuomo, OKXICE’s co-chairman and former New York governor, previously described the objections as expected, with many companies rather “wait and see how it goes rather than be the first to participate,” he said during a press call last week. What just happened? One day after Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion to fuel its AI spending, Nvidia has confirmed it will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering. Team Green calls the move a strengthening of the companies' AI partnership, one that will deepen their collaboration on the Muse AI models.  When Meta announced its stock offering yesterday, it was reported that Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom had indicated interest in buying up to $5 billion worth of the company's shares collectively. The world's largest company by market cap has now confirmed its contribution. The original fundraising plans comprised roughly $35 billion in initial offerings and a separate $60 billion share-sale program, expected after Meta's new nonvoting Class C shares begin trading in early 2027. That later program remains subject to final terms. Reuters reports that Meta increased the overall fundraising figure to $97.5 billion on Tuesday. Nvidia says the expanded partnership will focus on improving training and inference performance across Muse and its family of models, while reducing the cost of running them. The companies claim Muse has delivered strong benchmark results and surging downloads since launch, though there are no included figures. There is, unsurprisingly, more Nvidia hardware involved. Meta plans to expand its deployment of Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs, alongside Spectrum-X Ethernet networking and BlueField-4 technology. The aim is to squeeze more performance from each watt and improve the movement of data across its infrastructure. The pair are also considering further work on Nvidia's OpenShell framework for deploying agents safely and Sentry for monitoring their behavior. Muse sits at the center of Mark Zuckerberg's push for personal superintelligence. Meta describes it as an agent that can take action across everyday services, from sending emails to booking travel, with users deciding how much access to grant it. Meta expects capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion this year, nearly all of which is fueling its AI infrastructure buildout. The tech giant's latest quarterly results showed revenue rising 26% to $64.6 billion. For Nvidia, investing in a customer that plans to deploy more of its hardware adds to more questions about circular financing across the AI industry, which comes down to chip suppliers backing the companies that buy their products. By Andreas Wiseman  Executive Editor, Film & International  EXCLUSIVE: A24‘s fantasy video game adaptation Elden Ring is heading to the American Film Market,  where it’ll be the biggest-budget stand-alone project ever on sale at a film or TV market.  	We hear from sources the budget is being pegged between $175 million-$200 million but closer to the latter, which takes the project beyond previous tentpoles that have hit markets, including the latest Hunger Games installment. Mel Gibson’s upcoming Resurrection of the Christ came with a near-$200M price tag but across two films.  Elden Ring is comfortably A24’s biggest-budget project to date and continues the studio’s trend of taking swings on bigger budgets.  	           	Currently in post, the Alex Garland-scripted and -directed action epic is the talk of the acquisitions community given its scale and ambition. We can reveal today that Amazon MGM Studios has pre-empted that interest by taking a bunch of international pay-1 streaming rights off the table in a big deal. The pact is understood to cover a large number of international markets, and sources speculate to us that it is easily worth tens of millions of dollars. We hear the deal could also potentially lead to interesting activations on Amazon’s Twitch platform.     			Watch on Deadline		       	Amazon is a natural partner for the project given its previous Lord of the Rings investment and flexibility when it comes to international dealmaking. A24, which is fully financing the movie, will have needed/wanted at least one studio partner at that budget. Some international buyers may be disappointed that all-rights aren’t on the table, but their risk now lessens. All-rights asking prices at that budget would have likely been record-breaking and eye-watering.  	The Elden Ring cast includes Kit Connor, Ben Whishaw, Cailee Spaeny, Tom Burke, Havana Rose Liu, Sonoya Mizuno, Jonathan Pryce, Ruby Cruz and Nick Offerman. The A-list creative team includes costume designer Jenny Beavan, hair and makeup designer Paul Gooch, and production designers Mark Digby and Michelle Day. David J Thompson is DoP.  	           	Garland wrapped over the summer and is now in post with Industrial Light & Magic. Release is set for March 2028 in theaters and Imax.  	The script has been closely guarded in the period leading up to next month’s AFM in Los Angeles in ways generally reserved for the biggest IP. In what seems to be an industry first, A24 is flying members of its team directly to international buyers for them to read the script with the staffer present. It’s a long read; we hear it runs to at least 180 pages with visuals, implying the movie could push towards three hours.  	While plot details are largely being kept under wraps, we understand that in-demand Heartstopper actor Connor is the protagonist and the “faithful” film will follow his journey. There are said to be battles between his character and impressive monsters and dragons. But such is the secrecy around the project that parts of the script are being held back from buyers in what is presumably a bid to avoid spoilers and increase intrigue. There is due to be some kind of presentation at the AFM, potentially with footage.  	Released to critical acclaim in 2022, the role-playing game from Japanese publisher Bandai Namco is set in a dark fantasy world and allows players to head off on adventures within vast environments and dungeons. The main aim is to journey across “The Lands Between” to defeat the corrupted demigods (known as Shardbearers) and repair the shattered Elden Ring to become the Elden Lord. Created under the guidance of FromSoftware’s Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game is based on a story written by Game of Thrones originator George R.R. Martin.  Newly minted Netflix CCO Peter Rice is producing the movie alongside Andrew Macdonald and Allon Reich from DNA, as well as Martin and Vince Gerardis.  	Since its release, the game has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide and received dozens of awards. It ranks among the highest-rated games of all time and had one of the biggest debuts in Twitch history.   	The expectation from sources we’ve spoken to, and on fan forums, is that if the movie goes well, there would likely be a sequel; it’s prime fare to become a franchise. But that’s a long way down the line and we’ve heard nothing so far about a sequel being in the works. Elden Ring would need to make a lot of money for that to come to pass. Garland and A24 are first teaming on a Zendaya sci-fi film due to shoot in 2027.  	Meanwhile, the fast-ascending Connor is on course to have Elden Ring and the next X-Men movie — he is set to play Cyclops — both releasing in 2028, which could catapult him to tier 1 stardom. Hell, even Street Fighter is all falling victim to the same hubris.  As a fan of this game, I understand well that it is a derivative of Dark Souls, notorious for its impossible gameplay. The storyline is damn near impossible to follow and convoluted to the point that, even I, a fan, does not know the first thing when it comes to the lore of Elden Ring, nor Dark Souls. The story is not the point. It is the play. Same with all of the above mentioned, VERY NARRATIVELY LIGHT game IPs.  I do not foresee this going well for A24 simply because this is not a narrative driven IP. They will need to fabricate plot and LED Wall this thing straight into the ground. 2 terrible starting ingredients for any video game IP. From the above mentioned games, Elden Ring might have the smallest fanbase. We’ll add that as #3 for why this is not a good swing of the risk bat.  All of these movies failed for the reasons that I think Elden Ring is in dire danger of also failing for – zero narrative. For me to enjoy a game and keep playing it a compelling story is primary to me. Second is progression and customization which I’m pretty sure this game has. The third is I hate the game design trope where you have next to zero chance of succeeding the first time and have to try multiple times to accomplish it. It’s not so much the difficulty that bothers me just what feels like endless staring at load screens. The point of my post is should I continue to avoid this game as it’s prowa waste of money for me or should I give it a shot? it is the story of Vyke the original Tarnished New Line should have done it. Author of the First Trade newsletter They say good things come in pairs. The IPO market will be hoping that's true as Anthropic prepares to go public on the heels of SpaceX's record-shattering offering earlier this year. SpaceX had the fine distinction of rewriting the IPO record book. Anthropic now has a chance to do the same. And given the company's position near the heart of the AI trade, its debut could be an even bigger test of investor appetite. A warm reception could revive enthusiasm for AI stocks. A weak one could send ripples well beyond Anthropic. Let's break down the key numbers from Anthropic's brand new S-1 filing, along with some reported figures attached to the offering. They're listed in decreasing order. This is Anthropic's reported total addressable market, or theoretical future revenue opportunity, according to the WSJ. It was pitched to prospective investors rather than disclosed in the S-1, which offers no numerical TAM estimate. The figure would top the $28.5 trillion market opportunity SpaceX laid out ahead of its IPO. The reported upper end of the valuation Anthropic could seek when it prices. The figure is still fluid, since the S-1 didn't provide a share count nor a price range. But a $2 trillion valuation would surpass SpaceX's $1.74 trillion post-IPO value and place Anthropic in the top tier of public companies. The reported top end of Anthropic's potential IPO deal size. If the offering reaches that amount, it would become the largest ever, topping SpaceX's $75 billion raise. Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026, widening from $13 billion a year earlier. But there's an asterisk: About $72 billion of the total reflected a noncash accounting charge tied to the company's convertible financing. Revenue, meanwhile, kept ripping higher… The company's revenue in the first six months of 2026, up from $1.2 billion the year before. How much money Anthropic spent on computing and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, a nearly 300% increase from the same period in 2025. Text of this article October 27, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple Creator Studio adds powerful new AI features and even more creative tools Updates bring built-in MotionVFX content to Final Cut Pro, video assets in the Content Hub, expanded music creation tools to Logic Pro, and new intelligence features to Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages, and Numbers CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today introduced transformative updates to Apple Creator Studio, the powerful collection of creative apps designed to put studio-grade tools into the hands of modern creators across Mac, iPad, and iPhone. Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX — an expansive collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates, and motion graphics tools — as well as seamless editing in Pixelmator Pro. Apple’s curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro. Music creators using Logic Pro for Mac gain a new intelligent assistant in beta,1 an enhanced Stem Splitter that now separates drums, and a redesigned Browser that incorporates all sounds, with music understanding and even a Splice library. Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language. Keynote, Pages, and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants2 that understand document context and new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support for workflow automation.3 They also add stock video in the Content Hub and new premium themes and templates. Apple Creator Studio updates will be available on the App Store this November as a free update for existing subscribers.4 “This is our most exciting update since the launch of Apple Creator Studio. MotionVFX content in Final Cut Pro gives subscribers rapid access to extensive professional video effects and content, bringing incredible value to the suite,” said Brent Chiu-Watson, Apple’s senior director of Worldwide Product Marketing for Apps and iCloud. “Logic Pro’s new Browser allows users to explore and experiment with more sounds than ever as they create music. Pixelmator Pro’s sophisticated fill capabilities now let users completely reimagine any part of an image. And the assistant capabilities in Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages, and Numbers are going to change the game for how people interact with and learn to use these apps.” Expansive New Creative Toolkits and Video Workflows Final Cut Pro for Mac and iPad delivers an exceptional set of new capabilities for video editors, content creators, and filmmakers, from emerging storytellers to seasoned professionals deep in complex edits. Final Cut Pro for Mac now integrates MotionVFX directly into the app, giving editors access to thousands of elements, including templates with unique themes, stylish graphics, titles, and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking, and color grading. Editors can also tap into the Content Hub directly within Final Cut Pro and access a library of Apple-curated stock videos, photos, and backgrounds to fill gaps, add polish, or spark new ideas without leaving their workflow. Cross-app workflows and visual creation also take a major leap forward in Final Cut Pro. Editors can open any image from their timeline directly in Pixelmator Pro, take advantage of advanced editing tools, and save changes back to the project automatically — no reimporting required. With advanced image generation, users can create stunning images from text descriptions right inside their project, apply quick edits, and adjust visual styles. And Final Cut Pro introduces powerful workflow improvements, including more keyframe easing options for finer animation control, the ability to disconnect clips from the primary storyline to place them anywhere on the timeline, and 23 new transcription languages, making it easier than ever to caption and search footage. Motion also adds a built-in set of powerful MotionVFX plug-ins for cinematic color grading, 3D camera tracking, and one-click selection for stunning visual effects. Users can now generate and edit images from text descriptions, send images round-trip to Pixelmator Pro, fine-tune keyframe easing, and apply an all-new Displacement filter. Additionally, Compressor introduces the ability to encode Cinematic mode video recorded on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Reimagined Image Editing  Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, a powerful new tool to edit images based on a user’s description. Creators can simply circle an area in an image and describe the change they want. For more precision, creators can use existing Pixelmator Pro selection tools, like Free Selection, Quick Selection, or Magnetic Selection. Generate Fill automatically matches the lighting, perspective, and texture of the surrounding environment so edits blend in seamlessly, while built-in Super Resolution upscales the generated content so it stays sharp at any size. Generated elements can be merged into existing layers or inserted as new layers with intelligent masking that allows for continued refinement. Taking Music Creation Even Further  Logic Pro for Mac and iPad brings sophisticated, intuitive new tools for beat making, songwriting, remixing, and production. It also gets an all-new design featuring Liquid Glass, with translucent surfaces and deeper contrast that highlight waveforms and tracks. A new intelligent assistant powered by a combination of Apple-built and third-party models joins Logic Pro for Mac, helping creators and producers navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.¹ Finding the perfect sound is faster and more intuitive than ever with a redesigned Browser on Mac that centralizes loops, instruments, effect patches, and more. Powered by music understanding — an on-device audio analysis tool — Logic Pro automatically analyzes, classifies, and tags added sounds so creators can easily search their entire collection or drag in a loop to surface matching audio. Logic Pro’s industry-leading Stem Splitter gets even more advanced, with the ability to isolate, replace, or rebalance drum parts without needing the original multitracks. Users can also unlock a new Producer Pack from the 20-time Grammy winner and visionary widely known as the King of Modern Salsa, Sergio George. In this Producer Pack, George opens up his toolbox with his signature piano sound and authentic Latin jazz and salsa loops, including a full salsa percussion section, brass ensemble, and basses. With Voice Memo Studio Sound, users can also reduce room ambience and background noise in recordings captured on supported iPhone models, with the option to continue fine-tuning in Logic Pro. Powering Productivity with In-App Intelligence  Visual productivity apps receive a new generation of intelligence features for subscribers, including an intelligent assistant, built on Apple models and OpenAI, directly within Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant understands document context to help users accomplish more without leaving their work.² In Keynote, the intelligent assistant helps with designing, animating, and refining slides. In Pages, it drafts, restructures, and fine-tunes written content. In Numbers, it calculates, visualizes, and organizes data; recommends suitable chart types with a one-tap preview; and builds custom tables using world knowledge. New MCP support, built on this platform, enables external AI agents and tools to read content, perform edits, and execute automated actions directly in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. More Creative Options and Formats Across Keynote, Pages, and Numbers, the Content Hub expands to include Apple-curated stock video footage, giving creators dynamic visuals to enhance presentations, reports, and spreadsheets. Subscribers also gain access to a fresh collection of professionally designed templates and themes. Keynote introduces support for Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), an open JSON-based bundle file format designed to be readable and accessible to external tools, developer workflows, and AI agents. Freeform adds text styles for one-step formatting and reuse across boards, custom and preset board background colors, and, arriving in December, the ability to edit images directly in Pixelmator Pro and generate editable shapes from text descriptions. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Edward Tian, the 26-year-old cofounder of GPTZero, who's based in New York. His words have been edited for length and clarity. I was never planning to go down the founder path straight out of college. I had a visual investigations fellowship lined up for after graduation and was ready to start a journalism career. My cofounder Alex and I went to high school together. When ChatGPT came out, he was pursuing his Ph.D. in computer science at the University of Toronto, and I was in my senior year at Princeton. Over winter break, we built an AI detection tool and put it online. The success was almost overnight. Three years later, we sold our company, GPTZero, to Superhuman, and have stayed on board to work with the team. Superhuman is a very pro-AI company, and I think it was an unexpected move for us as an AI detection company to join them. We didn't build GPTZero to say there should be no AI on the internet. I think that's the biggest misunderstanding about why we started our company, but my feelings on AI have changed. Business Insider wants to talk to founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents, to understand what the "Tiny Teams" era really feels like — the wins, the fears, and the human skills that stand out. Share your story by filling out this quick form. I studied computer science at Princeton and worked with a professor at the Princeton Natural Language Processing Lab on AI research. I also worked on a few other startup projects in school, but I was always hoping to work in journalism. While in college, I became very involved in the open-source investigation community. I ended up working on open-source investigative projects with the BBC and Bellingcat, and had a visual investigations fellowship at The New York Times lined up after graduation, which I was excited about but ultimately didn't take. After ChatGPT came out, I was inspired to investigate where and when AI was being used online. It took about a week over winter break to build the first version of our AI detection tool, and it was released in January 2023. My cofounder Alex and I posted on social media to market the tool so people could try it, but we didn't view it as a business right away. However, it blew up online pretty quickly. After seeing the success, we wanted to double down on the opportunity and turn it into a legitimate site.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    One piece of advice I have for founders is that using a waitlist is really helpful for generating hype and excitement. We put the first version of GPTZero on a waitlist because it had reached capacity. So I think that artificial scarcity was also very helpful in the success. We had a lucky combination of very talented engineers and some traction and buzz, so we started reaching out to VCs. Many of our early VC partners went to my alma mater, and kind of all knew each other. Jack Altman is also an investor, and I remember we had a call where I was in my dorm room, and he was like, "Oh, I recognize that dorm room too." For founders raising funding for the first time, my advice is not to optimize for the flashiest name or the biggest brand because you think it will attract future talent. Go for where there's familiarity and trust; trust is the most important thing when working with an investor. We raised around $3.5 million in our first funding round. I stayed at Princeton to finish my senior year and graduate, and we kept growing the business. My cofounder Alex left his Ph.D. program to focus on the business. When Shishir, the new CEO of Superhuman, joined in 2025, we spoke with him about his broader platform vision for a suite of products. He thought we could be part of the authenticity suite he wanted to create. It was bittersweet to think about giving up something that we started from scratch and put so much energy and care into. At the same time, it was a lot easier because the team stayed on. I'm now a director of product at Superhuman. For company acquisitions, a lot of folks think the three most important things for a great fit are product match, people fit, and economic sense. We had similar people philosophies, and the deal made sense financially. Then, product-wise, we realized we're definitely not against AI use anywhere in education. We just want to make sure there's some authenticity and truth with that usage. Over the next few years, we're going to take our shot at building a startup within a larger company. I've seen a lot of startup founders go to larger companies and start their moonshots from within. The bigger mission we have is to take steps to ensure people are being respectful of the person who's on the receiving end of AI generations and productivity now. We want it to be that we're reaping the benefits of AI without making other people deal with more work. When we first started GPTZero, I think I was actually more pro-AI than I am now. I believe people should know when something is AI-generated, but I wasn't saying not to outsource anything at all. In the past year, though, I've started to see an over-reliance on AI among people who finished university after ChatGPT was launched, especially with writing. If I went back to college right now, I wouldn't major in computer science. I'd probably major in journalism and get a minor in computer science. I'd get a humanities degree because those are the important skills now. I've started to see a friction point at work when people can't write or edit, and everything they send reads like AI. Part of what I'm doing now at Superhuman is working on responsible AI usage policies and guidance. People are allowed to use these tools however they see fit. At the same time, I feel a profound sadness for the internet at large. It's important to make sure we still have human-written content online. US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe Biden The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is. It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them. Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge. During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices. "When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said. Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.  Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs. Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high. The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies. The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills. US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall. Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working. Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis". Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told", external, arguing that "nobody is getting fired". US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising. Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%. That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy. For Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar. Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things. "When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says. "When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was." Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently   The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day. Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators. "You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says. That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's. Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks. Trump has less room to do that. Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran. "The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans. "It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it." Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers. A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%. Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US households The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others. Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets. The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures. Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress. The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough. Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can. If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself. Mini LED is a new technology for Microsoft, and it's causing a bit of a stir on the new Surface Laptop Ultra. Here's what you need to know.  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Does the Mini LED display on Surface Laptop Ultra support local dimming? Many reviewers have noted the Mini LED display on Laptop Ultra is somewhat underwhelming, with ghosting issues and poor color contrast (albeit with great color accuracy) compared to other Mini LED screens on the market, and especially OLEDs. I said in my Surface Laptop Ultra review that its display features 1,344 local dimming zones, which is significantly lower than the dimming zones you'll find on a MacBook Pro with the same display tech. That results in a lot more ghosting and blooming, which can make the display feel stuttery and not smooth at times. Notebookcheck's review claimed the Surface Laptop Ultra's display doesn't feature any local dimming at all, which naturally caused a bit of an uproar online. So, what's the truth? Does the display support local dimming or not? I reached out to Microsoft again to see if it could clarify how the display works. The company told me that Surface Laptop Ultra does feature local dimming by default, with 5,400 LEDs across 1,344 dimming zones. Much like any other Mini LED display, these zones adjust backlight brightness based on the content in that area. If a bright window is being displayed on a black background, the dark areas of the screen will be dimmed. This behavior is what causes the ghosting and blooming effect on Surface Laptop Ultra, and is a side effect of Mini LEDs, especially ones with a low local dimming zone count. On my Surface Laptop Ultra in SDR, I can see the local dimming zones brightening and darkening as I move around a white window on a black background.      So, the display definitely does have local dimming capabilities. But it must be said that its performance isn't amazing compared to other Mini LEDs on the market. Whether local dimming is even working also depends entirely on your PCs settings. The local dimming behavior is controlled by a setting in Windows Settings under System > Display > Brightness. With "Change brightness based on content" enabled, and the "Enhanced" display profile set, the local dimming support should function. I've also found that you should turn off HDR for local dimming to be most effective. When HDR is on, the backlight is much more noticeable on dark backgrounds, likely because HDR requires much more brightness. A positive side effect of this is that this pretty much fixes the ghosting issue at the expense of local dimming performance. So, the TL:DR is Surface Laptop Ultra does feature local dimming capabilities. You should have HDR disabled, with "Change brightness based on content" enabled and the "Enhanced" display profile set in Windows Settings for it to be most effective. On the flipside, enabling HDR reduces the ghosting and blooming issues, but decreases local dimming performance. It must be said that the Mini LED display on Surface Laptop Ultra is somewhat disappointing. It certainly isn't as good as the Mini LED panel in a MacBook Pro, and I'm just left wondering why Microsoft didn't opt for OLED given that's what all the next-gen laptops are going with, including the upcoming MacBook Pro with touch. Maybe, hopefully, a future firmware update can adjust and improve the performance of the local dimming behavior on Surface Laptop UItra. The most recent firmware update did fix flickering issues that people were having with the display, so anything is possible. I've heard so many "Sir" stories come spewing out of Donald Trump's putrid mouth over the course of my career; I've truly lost track of them all. But this one might actually be the most bizarre yet.  Last night, the president made a pit stop in Corinth, Mississippi, where he attempted to give Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith a boost in her race against Democratic challenger Scott Colom. Polls have predicted Colom's defeat to Hyde-Smith in the deeply red state, but the margin is much slimmer than the GOP would hope for, due to the president's overall unpopularity in this country, especially with respect to his ongoing war with Iran that's left Americans holding a bag full of suffering with no recourse or end in sight.  In a level of true egotism and cowardice that only Donald Trump can really pull off, despite losing ground all across this country, the sitting president has focused his campaigning attention toward traditionally red, safe states, where the incumbent Republican candidates are struggling to keep their heads above water because he and his policies really suck that bad.  But, again, in true Trump fashion, Donald spent far more time harping and bragging on himself than the candidates he's supposed to be stumping for.  Last night, Trump stood at the podium and less-than-humbly bragged about the gains seen in the stock market since his return to office two years ago -- because we can all feed our families and fill our gas tanks with stock market gains, right?  "And since the election, the stock market has set 88 all-time record highs," he declared from the stage. "Think of that. That’s much less than two years. You know, we’re still, believe it or not, we’re still much less than two years. Nobody thought we could do this quickly. I didn’t even think we could do this quickly."  At that point, Trump urged the crowd to check on their 401 (k) accounts, which he claims are now doing so spectacularly, thanks to him, that it's saving marriages all across the country.  "But if you have any doubt, before you go and vote, pick up your 401(k)s and check it out. You see that you have made more money than you’ve ever made in your entire life, 60%, 65%, 58%," the president said.  And that's when the weird part came:  People are telling me right now, “My wife is in love with me. She thinks I’m like a great investor. Sir, my wife finally loves me. She thinks I’m a genius. ‘Darling, you’re really good at this, aren’t you?’ Yes, darling. Here, we’re up 64%.” Right? They didn’t do a damn thing. By AdExchanger Take The Wheel In June, Comcast made waves by announcing it would spin NBCUniversal into a separate public company (while retaining a fifth share of ownership for its first year). One lingering question has been what will happen to FreeWheel, Comcast’s TV and video ad server. The ad tech unit would make sense as part of either NBCU or Comcast proper.  But that question’s now resolved: FreeWheel will go with NBCU when the new company lists on the stock exchange next year, tipsheet.ai reports, citing internal Comcast communications.  “With advertising at the core of NBCUniversal, we believe closer alignment with ad technology will accelerate FreeWheel’s mission on behalf of the premium video ecosystem,” FreeWheel writes in a blog post confirming the news.  The cynical take is that Comcast has tasted the programmatic ads business and is spitting it back out. There’s plenty of precedent for that, actually. It’s basically what happened at AT&T (Xandr, we hardly knew ye) and during Verizon’s ill-fated Yahoo takeover (recall Yahoo’s proposed spin-off as Oath and the cringeworthy “Take the Oath” tagline). But Ari Paparo – who sold the DSP Beeswax to FreeWheel – tweeted, “I think the opposite. NBC really wants to own tech as part of their overall stack.” Getting There Retail media is oversaturated with standalone platforms. Cue the consolidation speculation.  Big global brands like Coca-Cola or Hershey that are sold everywhere log into hundreds of retailer interfaces whose data they can’t get elsewhere. Some of these long-tail retail media networks are contested by Criteo and other ad tech vendors.  But the top of the market is primed for blockbuster consolidation swings. The Trump administration is lenient if not borderline indifferent to acquisitions that might have drawn challenges by previous FTCs or DOJs. Kroger and Albertsons probably wish they’d waited on their disastrous failed merger. Given this environment, The Information’s report that Instacart is up for sale makes perfect sense. Instacart has reportedly been in talks with Uber and DoorDash, though apparently Uber has walked.  DoorDash previously considered an Instacart acquisition back in 2021 when the grocery delivery service was ad-free and a private venture-backed startup. Instacart was valued between $40 billion and $50 billion back then, whereas its public market cap is now $12 billion.  An acquisition by either DoorDash or Uber would consolidate a major niche in last-mile delivery and retail media margin-ification. Uber launched its ad biz in 2022 and surpassed a $1 billion run rate by 2024. DoorDash had its first billion-dollar ad year last year. Too-Smart TVs A viral post from this weekend is reigniting consumer fears that smart TVs are spying on us. An X poster by the name log4j, who claims to be a cybersecurity researcher, says they reverse-engineered the code behind their $3,000 Samsung TV using ChatGPT and other decompiling software. The hack revealed what log4j sardonically refers to as “PRIVACY HORROR”: an always-on mic that listens for barking dogs or crying babies. It then reports back to Samsung to better serve you ads. Adding fuel to the conspiratorial fire, log4j shared an email from OpenAI notifying them that their account was suspended for “Cyber Abuse” – invoking fears of Big Tech companies circling the wagons. But rather than something shady happening behind the scenes, the features are actually hyped in some of Samsung’s consumer marketing, Tech Radar reports. Samsung touted its listening tech as “family and pet care” that notified different devices if a loved one seemed in distress. Although Samsung apparently discontinued the baby-listening feature last month after it couldn’t tell whether a baby was crying on TV or in real life. Of course, Samsung could have made it clearer that it’s sending the data to its servers, and for what purpose, Tech Radar notes. But even consumer-facing features can take on a sinister light in the public’s eyes when they’re associated with surveillance advertising. But Wait! As a lover of all things NBN, I’m no stranger to the latest internet deals in Australia. More often than not, it’s the same handful of internet service providers that jostle for my top recommendation — those being Exetel, Kogan Internet, Superloop and Spintel, to name a few. One provider that, if my memory serves correctly, has never popped up on my radar is Telstra. Yes, despite dominating the NBN landscape with a 35.2% market share, Telstra isn’t exactly known for its affordability. In actuality, the nation’s flagship telco is often the most expensive of the 30 or so providers I monitor on a regular basis. Imagine my surprise when I learned that Telstra, of all companies, had actual deals on its NBN lineup, with up to AU$240 in savings over six months! And while they still don’t offer the cheapest NBN plans, they’re still worth shouting about if you’re in the market for a new NBN plan. What’s more, Belong, a generally more affordable NBN provider 100% owned by Telstra, also has some attractive deals right now, including laying claim to the cheapest introductory cost on the NBN 100/500 tier at AU$59/m. Do note that the most affordable Telstra NBN plans require you to BYO modem. If you want a Telstra Smart Modem 4, you’ll not only need to pay more each month, but you’ll also need to pay any remaining device payments if you cancel your plan within 24 months. Alternatively, you can buy the Telstra modem for a one-off fee of AU$360. However, for that money, I would recommend seeking out one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems in Australia instead. Telstra Premium | 500Mbps TES | AU$69/m (first 6 months, then AU$99/m) Shaving AU$30 off each month for the first six months, Telstra’s NBN 500 becomes a lot more attractive. Yes, it’s possible to spend less, but the fact that it comes in under the current average introductory cost of AU$74 is something to take notice of. Plus, the ongoing cost of AU$99 is roughly on par with the AU$95 average.  • AU$69 minimum cost• AU$1,008 first year cost• AU$1,188 ongoing yearly cost Belong NBN Fast | 500Mbps TES | AU$59/m (first 6 months, then AU$95/m) Alternatively, for AU$10 less each month for the first half-year, you can get Belong’s NBN 500 plan. This is the current cheapest introductory cost of any provider, and it even includes a free SIM card to access the Telstra Wholesale network, loaded with AU$80 credit.  • AU$59 minimum cost• AU$924 first year cost• AU$1,140 ongoing yearly cost Belong NBN Standard | 50Mbps TES | AU$55/m (first 6 months, then AU$91/m) The other speed tier where Belong claims the cheapest introductory cost is NBN 50, making it a tempting proposition for anyone who can comfortably get by with a slower connection. Of course, for just AU$4 more you could get the NBN 500 plan above (or NBN 100 if that’s the maximum available to you), which only highlights how much of a good deal it is.  • AU$55 minimum cost• AU$876 first year cost• AU$1,092 ongoing yearly cost Belong is 100% owned by Telstra and is a lower-cost alternative to the flagship brand. To offer more affordable mobile and NBN plans compared to Telstra, it makes some compromises where features and network coverage are concerned. In the case of mobile, Belong uses the Telstra Wholesale Network, which is said to cover around 98.8% of the population, compared to the full Telstra network that enjoys 99.7% coverage. In the case of NBN, however, both providers use the same underlying fixed-line network, so coverage isn't a differentiating factor. Actual speeds can still vary between providers, depending on how much capacity they have available and how their networks are managed, particularly during busier periods. However, there's no guarantee Telstra will deliver faster speeds than Belong on an equivalent plan. Belong keeps its costs lower by making some trade-offs, including giving customers the option to bring their own modem or purchase one separately. In either case, there’s no option for installation help. Telstra also supports BYO modems, but offers its own Smart Modem with 4G backup, a feature Belong doesn't provide. There are also some differences with technical support. Telstra offers 24/7 phone support and live chat, and has physical stores. Belong works on a digital-only basis, with support limited to online chat or messages via the website or app. There is limited phone support should you need it.
