Search The Points Guy Could high jet fuel costs and financial challenges force JetBlue to pause its push to add premium products, such as first-class seats? CEO Joanna Geraghty left no ambiguity in her answer: "Absolutely not." That line of questioning, which came during the carrier's quarterly earnings call Tuesday, was fair. And Geraghty's answer was critically important to both passengers and investors. New details dropped by executives during the call offer a first glimpse of how those new premium products are already performing. JetBlue has struggled to turn a steady profit. A heavy debt load coupled with planned capital investments — including the airline's push to add premium amenities — helped stoke speculation that a restructuring could be in the cards for the airline. That comes as the airline's bonds have been losing value and as its stock price hit an all-time low Monday. "I think there is a significant disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results are demonstrating," Geraghty pushed back on Tuesday's call. More broadly, JetBlue reported a $257 million net loss for the three months ending Sept. 30 and cited a fuel bill that was up nearly two-thirds from the same time last year. Still, JetBlue executives expect to reach a sustainable profit by 2028 as the company doubles down on its "JetForward" turnaround plan. Already, the executives said, the plan is showing encouraging signs, such as better revenue than expected this past quarter amid strong consumer demand. JetForward focuses on realigning the airline's network around East Coast leisure routes and growing Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) as a focus city. It also includes the introduction of new premium products to help the airline earn the premium revenue bonus that has enabled other major carriers, particularly Delta Air Lines and United Airlines, to thrive — even amid higher costs. While volatile fuel costs linked to the war in the Persian Gulf continue to pressure the airline, JetBlue executives pointed to a lengthy financial cushion that it can use to continue the premium investment. This includes things like installing new first-class seats on aircraft, operating lounges and upgrading airport amenities. The airline has $2.2 billion in liquidity available, plus another $7 billion in unencumbered assets, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines. For more than a decade, JetBlue has offered Mint business class on certain key transcontinental routes — followed later on transatlantic service. But BlueFirst will be the airline's first foray into a true domestic first class. The first BlueFirst seats went on sale earlier this month, with the first flight scheduled between Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) and FLL for Dec. 8. The airline will introduce the cabin on 38 more routes by April, and will offer BlueFirst on a "majority" of its planes by the end of 2027. The installation program across JetBlue's fleet is slated for completion in 2028. More: JetBlue says domestic Mint flyers can now access its lounges, too During the earnings call, airline president Marty St. George said JetBlue is "encouraged" by the early response to BlueFirst, particularly the overlap between TrueBlue frequent flyer members and the new seats. About 35% of bookings for BlueFirst so far were made using miles, St. George noted, while Mosaic elite members accounted for roughly a quarter of seats booked to date. "Our favorite fact is seeing how many of the seats are being sold to our existing customers," he said. "While still early, this engagement reinforces our confidence in BlueFirst's ability to capture more premium travel demand from our existing loyal customer base." The loyalty program has been an important revenue driver for JetBlue, St. George noted. This, coupled with current booking trends, underscores the importance of the premium pivot in keeping passengers loyal and engaged with TrueBlue. Revenue from the program was up 20% compared to last year. "Our investments in premium products and partnerships are driving deeper brand loyalty and engagement," St. George said, "with record levels of active TrueBlue members and elite status qualifications this quarter." JetBlue's new BlueHouse lounges, which opened at New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in late 2025 and at BOS over the summer of 2026, have been a meaningful driver of the loyalty program, St. George noted. Signups for JetBlue's premium cobranded credit card, which lets cardholders enter the lounges before a JetBlue flight, increased eightfold compared to last year. Meanwhile, spending across the entire credit card portfolio grew by "double digits." One of the big catalysts for that increase in spending, St. George said, is the airline's Blue Sky partnership with United, which lets members use TrueBlue miles on United flights and vice versa and allows for reciprocal elite perks. JetBlue members can earn elite status credit from JetBlue flights, but — to the consternation of United flyers — not the other way around. Within that partnership, the list of United destinations available to travelers using TrueBlue miles has grown to include a broad list of international destinations, fixing what St. George described as "a shortcoming of the program, historically." JetBlue's plan to double down on FLL in the wake of Spirit Airlines' shutdown has been largely successful, JetBlue executives said, even as the airline continues to grow routes from the Florida focus city. Unit revenue was up at the airport, while JetBlue's capacity there has grown 65% compared to the same period last year, with the airline planning to continue scaling up. The airline's seat share in the market will reach around 37% by the end of this year, up nearly 15% from the same period last year. Meanwhile, cobranded card signups in South Florida are up 55%, Geraghty said. JetBlue is carrying a lot of debt and has been hit especially hard by increasing fuel prices and bad weather along the East Coast during the summer. But the airline sees its pivot to premium as its best way forward to financial security. Despite the current financial pressures, executives plan to stay the course and grow into its realigned network while expanding its premium offerings as quickly as possible. So far, signs suggest that the arguments laid out by JetBlue's management are convincing. The airline's shares rallied on Tuesday, up around 20% to counteract Monday's slide. At least one financial analyst seemed to agree. In a research note following the call, Melius Research airline analyst Conor Cunningham described the tone of JetBlue's executives as "constructive." "Taking a step back, the plan JetBlue has been trying to execute is a rational one," Cunningham wrote. "But the plan requires time, and its progress has been largely masked by erratic shifts in the macro." Login  Vlad  27 October 2026   Motorola Android  Motorola showed off the Signature 27 at Qualcomm's Snapdragon event last month, but it hasn't revealed the full specs or pricing yet. Now, Portuguese retailer MegaPC has listed the Motorola Signature 27, and reportedly the upcoming Motorola Razr Flex as well. The Signature 27 is listed in the Pantone Coal Smoke color with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage for €1,594.90. The page is currently marked as temporarily out of stock, and there's no word on when it will ship. The description mostly repeats what Motorola has already said: the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, a 200MP periscope telephoto camera, a 50MP Sony Lytia 910 main camera, and audio tuned by Bang & Olufsen. It also mentions an aerospace-grade aluminum frame, ceramic glass, and a 3D vapor chamber for cooling. For reference, this is the successor to the Motorola Signature that launched earlier this year. The Razr Flex is the more interesting part. It appeared in two separate listings, one for the Pantone Coriander color and one for Pantone Dark Botanical Garden, both with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage for €1,510.90. Those colors match what we've heard about the wide foldable before, which has also shown up on Geekbench recently with a Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chipset and Android 17. Michael Burry isn't the only trader made famous by "The Big Short" who's bearish on big names in the AI trade. Seawolf Capital, the investment firm founded by three traders featured in the book and film said on Friday that it is short CoreWeave, the neocloud company that's seen its stock price swoon in recent weeks amid concerns about its debt. Co-founder Vincent Daniel says that Seawolf's short bet against the neocloud began with a social media post. More specifically, it started with someone on X mocking investors who were shorting CoreWeave but with no analysis of the company's financials. "Hard to disagree with that sentiment, so we decided to put pen to paper and take a look," Daniel wrote in a Substack article. "As we went down the rabbit hole of the CoreWeave story, we started to realize that their business model looked very familiar." Vincent, along with Seawolf co-founders and fellow traders Danny Moses and Porter Collins, examined CoreWeave in depth, examining its neocloud business model that centers around leasing out AI computing power enabled by high GPUs, primarily those made by Nvidia. Daniel said that CoreWeave's business model called to mind numerous other companies that buy up specific assets and lease them out to customers. Such companies include Transocean, which leases drilling rigs to oil companies, and aviation equipment leasing company AerCap Holdings. Seawolf noted that it maintains positions in both firms, but emphasized that it prefers them over CoreWeave, as GPUs may not have as long an economic life as oil drills, airplanes, or shipping equipment. "We favor renting assets where underlying supply is structurally constrained and forward order books are modest," he stated. "While demand for compute is undeniably robust, the forward supply of competing chip capacity is expanding at a breakneck pace." On top of that, for CoreWeave's operations to continue, Seawolf said that it would require signifiant capital to continue purchasing high-priced AI chips. "Based on projected 2027 free cash flow deficits and current balance-sheet leverage (specifically tangible common equity to total assets), the setup is daunting," Daniel noted. "To own this equity, an investor must underwrite that CoreWeave can raise tens of billions of dollars in incremental capital on accretive terms—not a bet we are willing to take." Daniel added, though, that Seawolf is still in the "early innings" of its CoreWeave analysis. This isn't the first time that the firm has raised concerns about CoreWeave. Early in October, Moses appeared on The Real Eisman playbook with fellow "Big Short" investor Steve Eisman, and compared it to WeWork, the former Silicon Valley office space unicorn now regarded as a cautionary tale for tech startups. Daniel added, though, that Seawolf doesn't regard its short position in CoreWeave as a bet against the the health of the broader AI trade. He said that he views it as a call on the availability and the cost of capital, noting that tech companies are competing with the government for financing and facing a tightening monetary cycle. In his view, this has led to a market in which AI companies may not be able to fund themselves affordably. "If it can't fund itself cheaply, or if the capital is really not available, it's going to be hard to finish this through, and that's kind of the call I'm making on CoreWeave," Daniel told Business Insider. Featured Reviews Featured Community Stories Featured Credit Cards JetBlue is obviously in a tough financial spot. The airline hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic, and is approaching $9 billion in debt, which is just not sustainable in the long run. It sure seems like a trip into Chapter 11 bankruptcy is in the cards — the CEO has insisted it won’t happen in 2026, but I think that’s about the only thing that can be promised. Anyway, JetBlue has just released its Q3 2026 results, and there’s quite a bit of optimism in there… including a claim that JetBlue will turn an operating profit in 2027?! In this post: JetBlue has posted a net loss of $257 million in Q3 2026, with an operating loss of $144 million, meaning the operating margin was negative 5.1%. Admittedly it has been a tough year for all carriers, given the increase in jet fuel prices. While airlines have been able to increase fares somewhat, it hasn’t been enough to fully offset the increase in costs. For context, below are JetBlue’s operating income and margin over the past seven quarters, since the beginning of 2025. That amounts to close to $900 million in operating losses over seven quarters. While JetBlue’s stock has been in a downward spiral in recent times, given the likely possibility of a Chapter 11 filing, the carrier’s Q3 2026 release are sending the stock up significantly pre-market, despite a slight revenue and earnings per share miss. What’s the great news from JetBlue? Well, CEO Joanna Geraghty is confident the airline will turn an operating profit in 2027: “I’m very encouraged by the progress we made in the third quarter. Resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue well ahead of our initial expectations, allowing us to recapture more of the increase in fuel costs than we initially expected. That momentum has carried into the fourth quarter, and Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver exceptional results even as we significantly grow capacity.” “We delivered year-over-year adjusted operating margin improvement in the third quarter and expect further expansion in the fourth quarter even with higher fuel prices. Together with continued JetForward execution, this reinforces our confidence in achieving sustained operating profitability in 2027 and delivering at least $1 EPS and positive free cash flow in 2028.” Let me emphasize that an operating profit and a net profit are not the same thing. JetBlue is currently paying around $600 million per year in interest expenses. However, an operating profit would of course be major progress. The question is, is this just baseless optimism on the part of JetBlue, or what’s going on? It’s of course great to claim that the airline will turn an operating profit in 2027, though the math isn’t really mathing for me here. Yes, I think JetBlue is making some generally positive changes, like rolling out first class, and increasingly leaning into its loyalty program, including opening lounges. However, the carrier’s margins are (understandably) getting worse rather than better, so I don’t really see how anyone can make the claim about profitability in 2027, other than just pure hope and optimism. Broadly speaking, it feels like many industry executives are basically taking the approach of thinking that jet fuel prices will decrease materially, all while airlines will be able to maintain the fare increases they’ve been able to push through since the start of the war. I do feel like JetBlue management has lost a bit of credibility when it comes to their claims about JetForward and profitability. In early 2025, the company’s CFO claimed the airline expected to reach a positive operating margin in 2025. Obviously that didn’t happen. Then in early 2026, the company’s management said it expected a breakeven or positive operating margin for 2026. Obviously that didn’t happen either. Admittedly many issues were due to macro trends beyond the carrier’s control, but that’s also just a reality of the industry. So I’d view the 2027 operating profit goal as being one based on perfect macro conditions, with airlines able to maintain the same pricing power with much lower fuel prices. This is overly simplistic, but just to put this into perspective: If we were to assume that both airlines saw a 6.6% increase in operating margins, American would have an operating profit of over $3.6 billion, putting it in Delta’s league. Those are some fanciful projections, eh? JetBlue’s Q3 2026 margins worsened, which isn’t surprising, given the impact of jet fuel prices on airlines. What I find interesting is that JetBlue executives claim the airline will turn an operating profit in 2027. Admittedly they’ve been trying to make these claims for a couple of years now, but I just struggle to follow that logic, unless we’re to believe that jet fuel prices will go down materially, while airlines will be able to maintain fare increases. Operating profit or not, JetBlue will have to find a way to shed its debt, if it ever stands a chance of turning a net profit, given how much it’s paying to service its nearly $9 billion in debt. China is both a threat to Anthropic — and a warning about AI bubbles  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  As AI firm Anthropic gears up for an enormous $2 trillion initial public offering (IPO) that could be the largest in stock market history, the company's prospectus has just warned that AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Yet there might be a very different kind of danger on the horizon, as an early warning from China hints that its AI bubble might be about to burst. In papers filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Anthropic outlined some of the risks facing the company and its investors. It detailed a long list of factors that could impact its business, including not being able to access enough compute power to maintain its workloads, inaccurately forecasting how much power it needs (and thus over- or underpaying for hardware), failures in its supply chain that might leave it without adequate resources, and many more. One of the more startling sections of the document outlines how Anthropic’s AI models could accelerate beyond anyone’s ability to evaluate and safeguard them and “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.” Aside from the obvious danger posed to humanity, Anthropic is also apparently worried that such an outcome could “adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” That situation could be compounded by AI models’ “unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information", Anthropic said. AI could also "generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model’s continued operation or access,” the company added. As Anthropic notes, some of these possibilities have become reality, and it’s that sort of eventuality that has prompted another threat to its business: public backlash. “Opposition to data center development has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions,” the company wrote, and that doesn’t seem to be going anywhere as negative headlines continue to proliferate. Another eye-opening passage concerns Anthropic’s need to continually secure funding for its operations. The company has posted increasingly huge losses every year that it has operated — including $1.5 billion in 2023, $8.3 billion in 2024, $42 billion in 2025, and $80 billion in just the first six months of 2026 — and is reliant on continued venture capital inflows. Anthropic’s IPO listing notes that “it is critical that we maintain strong revenue growth” but that “our revenue growth may not be sustainable … We expect our costs will increase over time and our losses will continue.” How sustainable it is to lose more than $80 billion in just six months on a continual basis remains to be seen. While Anthropic has been postulating on what might happen to its business — and the world — if any of these forecasts come to pass, we’re already seeing that in action in China. According to a report from Reuters, the Chinese AI bubble has already burst, with the STAR50 stock index dropping 40% in four months and taking with it $480 billion in market value. Rather than a single catalyzing factor, the precipitous fall has been fueled by concerns about high prices, AI demand, and the impact of tariffs and bans on Chinese exports, Reuters reported. Shares in robotics firm Unitree have halved in value since listing in August, for example, while chipmaker CXMT’s stocks are down more than 25% in a month. Other firms have seen similarly sizable drops. That includes MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads Technology, which jumped 700% and 400% on their initial listings but have now “halved in value since July.” As fund manager Wang ​Zhuo told Reuters, “All bubbles inevitably burst.” With Anthropic alerting readers to the serious threats posed to humanity by future AI developments, the situation in China provides another kind of warning: that the bubble might pop before any of that comes to pass. Asia’s fourth-largest economy grows 3.4 percent year-on-year amid strong semiconductor demand. Save Share South Korea’s economy grew much faster than expected in the July-September quarter amid booming demand for chips used in artificial intelligence (AI). Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1 percent on a quarterly basis, or 3.4 percent year-on-year, advance estimates released by the Bank of Korea showed on Tuesday. The Bank of Korea forecast in August that GDP would grow 0.3 percent in the third quarter. Exports, which account for about 45 percent of South Korea’s GDP, rose 2.3 percent quarter-on-quarter, driven by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment, according to the central bank. Investment in facilities and intellectual property rose 4.1 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively, while investment in construction edged up 0.7 percent. Despite the robust growth in exports and investment, private consumption fell 0.2 percent. The latest results put the South Korean economy well on track to achieve its biggest economic expansion in more than a decade. South Korean Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said earlier this month that he expected growth to reach 3.4-3.6 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest performance since 2011, excluding the COVID-19 pandemic. South Korea’s economy grew 1 percent in 2025, its slowest expansion since the pandemic. Asia’s fourth-largest economy has capitalised on the AI boom amid a global shortage of memory chips. South Korea is home to two of the three largest memory chip makers, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory. South Korea’s exports in September surged 83.5 percent year-on-year to $120.9bn, with chips accounting for nearly half of all shipments, according to the Korea Customs Service. Plaid Cymru ministers say they want extra cash for railways and public services in Wales ahead of the UK government's Budget on Wednesday. Welsh Finance Minister Elin Jones called for the Chancellor John Healey to set out a spending plan that "finally treats us fairly". The Budget announces Westminster's tax and spending plans for the year ahead - and more cash given to English public services could result in extra spending in Wales where they are devolved. A UK government spokesperson said the chancellor would focus on giving households and businesses "a bit of breathing space where we can".  Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase Healey to shield low-income pensioners from income tax in the Budget Meanwhile, shoppers in one of Wales' busiest markets told BBC Wales that once again the cost of living was their biggest concern before the spending announcement. Any extra spending for things in England that are controlled in Wales by the Welsh government - like healthcare, schools and roads - could trigger additional cash for the country. Elin Jones had asked the chancellor to bring forward Â£1bn of the Â£14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales. She also asked for extra money to help the Welsh government set its budget for 2027-28, which currently faces a real-term cut in day-to-day spending. She previously claimed Wednesday's settlement could be the worst for the Welsh government since the Covid-19 pandemic. Elin Jones says Wales needs a budget that treats the country "fairly" Jones said Wales had been short-changed "for years". "This UK Budget is the moment of truth, and we need the chancellor to act, not just acknowledge the problem," she said. "Wales pulls its weight in the UK economy. We contribute. Now we need the UK government to match that ambition with action and deliver a budget that finally treats us fairly." There have also been calls from Labour MP Nia Griffith to give the Welsh government greater flexibility to borrow to fund investment projects. A senior Welsh Labour source said they had been "pressing really hard for fiscal flexibility", along the lines of Griffith's request. Ahead of Wednesday's announcement, shoppers and traders at Swansea Market said the cost of living was their biggest concern. "Will we be able to see through the winter without having to borrow money," said shopper Louise. "It's quite a worry." Like others at the market, Louise admitted feeling "anxious" about the winter, despite having saved some money with her supplier.  Help with energy costs was the top of many people's lists of things they wanted help with in the Budget.  Prices rose at the beginning of the month and typical bills are forecast to increase by 16% in January because of the conflict in the Middle East. Louise says she is worried about the winter because "everything is getting more expensive" Dad-of-two Richard said his wage did not keep up with rising energy bills, leaving his family "penny pinching towards the end of the month". "Things that we used to have as a bit of luxury are out of the question, days out with family cost a fortune," he said. Rural homes that use heating oil have also seen a dramatic increase in costs. The chancellor had already announced he will remove import taxes to bring the price down a little. Healey has talked about giving people "breathing space" from cost-of-living pressures, and revealed a package of small measures he is calling "everyday fixes" ahead of the Budget. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also wants to cut standing charges from gas bills. If further support is offered in the Budget, it would be likely limited and targeted to the poorest households. Richard, from Swansea, says "a lot of things that used to be affordable are now out of reach" The cost of filling up cars soared this year as the conflict in the Middle East pushed up the price of oil. Petrol prices hit a four-year high in September, and diesel has also shot up. The cost of transporting fruit and veg is one issue putting pressure on Gareth Evans, who is the fourth generation of his family to run the Get Fresh stall at Swansea Market. "It's a struggle at the moment," he said. "We get costs passed on to us from our suppliers. "We've also got vans ourselves and we supply caterers and diesel is very expensive." Emma, who runs a pet store, said her rising costs meant she has had to increase prices for customers, as "it goes down the line". She believes many working people are "struggling to live now". The chancellor is expected to freeze the planned increase in fuel duty in January. The rate was reduced by 5p by the previous Conservative government in 2022 and that measure has already been extended twice. Gareth took over the running of the family fruit and veg stall from his dad Chris who had worked there for 50 years One of Elin Jones' requests is for the UK government's help for a flagship scheme to help address child poverty. The Welsh government is planning a trial scheme paying 15,000 children in families on universal credit Â£10 a week. The Cynnal scheme, external is modelled on the Scottish government's child payment which helped to reduce child poverty in Scotland. Welsh ministers have asked the UK government to exempt the payments from tax and benefits calculations, so recipients do not see a cut to their income. BBC Wales has been told discussions about the child payment are still ongoing, which suggests there will be no announcement on Wednesday. Burnham had previously said he was "open" to considering this, and it has already been granted to facilitate the scheme in Scotland. The chancellor will also announce how much the state pension will increase by next year.  It looks likely to top Â£13,000 a year with the full, flat rate expected to increase by Â£488 a year in April due to the triple lock guarantee. One thing that has already been announced is that pensioners who rely entirely on the state pension will be shielded from paying income tax, which usually kicks in at Â£12,570. The specific details will be announced in the Budget. On working age welfare, Healey has been rolling the pitch to prepare Labour MPs for potential cuts to the benefits bill, with a carefully scripted speech at this year's party conference. There are reports that young people not in education, work or training may see big changes to their support, but that could be unveiled after the Budget when former Health Secretary Alan Milburn publishes his recommendations for reform. Reform UK Senedd member Cai Parry Jones said his party "would stop using Welsh people as cash cows", and would build an M4 relief road, scrap family farm tax, and "reward working people" by raising tax-free personal allowance to Â£15,000. Welsh Conservative Senedd leader Darren Millar called for the UK government to make money available for major road projects, including an M4 relief road, and more defence spending in Wales, calling for a "pro-union Budget deal". David Chadwick, Welsh Liberal Democrat MP, said his party wanted a Budget that gave Welsh families "some much-needed breathing space", calling for a 10p cut in fuel duty, a guarantee to bring down energy bills, and a temporary VAT cut for hospitality. The Budget comes ahead of the first substantive meeting between the prime minister and the first minister at the National Economic Council later this week, where devolution is expected to be discussed. A UK government spokesperson said: "The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That's why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, extended the 5p fuel duty cut and frozen rail fares." Bitcoin mining companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI), renting out computing power and converting mining facilities into data centers. Now, some of the companies that built their businesses serving bitcoin miners are following them into the AI market. Luxor Technology, best known for its bitcoin mining services, is also moving into AI hardware and trading contracts that allow companies to agree on computing prices in advance. The Seattle-based company said on Tuesday that it raised $16 million in a round led by CMT Digital. Bitcoin mining equipment makers Canaan and MicroBT also invested. Luxor said the money will go toward its AI hardware brokerage and computing-power trading business. The round included new investment and sales of existing shares, although Luxor did not disclose how much of the new funding was invested in the company. Publicly traded bitcoin miners had signed more than $70 billion worth of AI and high-performance computing contracts by the end of March, according to CoinShares data. Not everyone is moving away from bitcoin mining. Nasdaq-listed NIP Group (NIPG) announced plans last week to essentially increase its mining capacity by about 48%. The company said it expects to generate about 195 bitcoin a month at full deployment. Moving into AI also requires more than access to electricity. Ethan Vera, Luxor's chief operating officer, told CoinDesk that its software business works with bitcoin miners representing nearly two gigawatts of power capacity. After assessing more than half that capacity, Luxor found that most sites had sufficient electricity and fiber connections for AI workloads but would require new data centers. Luxor is also expanding into contracts that allow buyers and sellers to agree on future computing prices, much as bitcoin miners use financial contracts to manage changes in mining revenue. Sam Hallene, a partner at CMT Digital, said AI companies have different reasons to protect themselves against price changes, including the possibility that expensive computing equipment remains useful longer than expected. "We don’t know exactly what the market structure will look like at the end of the day," Hallene told CoinDesk. Luxor already offers privately negotiated contracts tied to computing rental prices, although the market is still developing. Vera said transparency remains a problem, particularly around AI hardware prices. In August, Luxor introduced a price index that tracks daily asking prices for Nvidia AI server systems, providing buyers and sellers with a reference point for equipment prices. November 19 will mark an event that some gamers have been waiting more than a decade for, but it should also be a date for investors to mark on their own calendars.  We're talking about the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, Rockstar Games' sprawling crime epic that's set to be the biggest video-game release in years. Fans are so excited for the new installment that some are already planning to take time off from work to play it on release day.  But according to Bank of America, investors should also get ready, as the game's release could be a growth-driving catalyst for Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of GTA's developer. "We recommend being long TTWO through the GTA 6 launch," BofA wrote in a note to investors. "It remains cheap on the LT growth we believe will soon become apparent." It hasn't been a good year for Take-Two so far. The company's portfolio also includes popular sports game franchise 2K, Gearbox Entertainment, and popular mobile game maker Zynga, but shares have dropped 21% year to date. BofA sees the stock's struggle in 2026 setting up an opportunity, citing the growth potential stemming from GTA, particular the monetization of its massively popular online mode, which the analysts say investors may be missing as they assess the company's earnings outlook. In the bank's view, online monetization potential for the GTA franchise is Take-Two's most important earnings driver on a long-term basis. "Our LT EPS growth forecast is materially stronger than what we've heard, and a GTA Online launch in 1CQ27 should begin providing tangible evidence of that monetization upside," BofA noted. "As that strength becomes apparent, we believe the market will need to revise its long-term EPS growth forecasts higher." For that reason, the bank reiterated its Buy rating on TTWO stock, and while it lowered its price target from $380 to $330, the new target still implies 62% upside potential. Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin is set to reach Robinhood’s retail customers later this year, giving the dollar-backed token access to a brokerage platform with roughly 28.6 million funded accounts. “From bringing RLUSD to retail and institutional markets to helping Robinhood manage its own treasury operations, this partnership reflects growing institutional demand for integrated solutions that support customer-facing offerings and core financial operations,” said Monica Long, president of Ripple. The companies announced the partnership on Tuesday. RLUSD is already available on Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, the crypto exchange Robinhood acquired for $200 million in June. Now, RLUSD is also expected to become available through the Robinhood app before the end of 2026. That decision puts Robinhood in an unusual position, as it helped establish the Global Dollar Network in 2024 to promote USDG, a competing stablecoin issued by Paxos. Now, Robinhood is announcing its plans to offer Ripple’s rival token to its customers. The Global Dollar Network, founded in 2024, brings together companies that help distribute USDG and share in the revenue it generates. The arrangement gives members a financial incentive to promote USDG, but Robinhood’s partnership with Ripple shows that those incentives do not preclude members from offering competing stablecoins. Other founding members included Kraken, Galaxy Digital, Anchorage Digital and CoinDesk's parent company, Bullish. Arbitrum joined earlier this month. Robinhood has already given USDG a role in its products. In July, the consortium announced that USDG would be the default lending asset for Robinhood Earn, its onchain lending product. Robinhood did not announce any changes to its USDG agreement, and it remains unclear whether RLUSD will be offered alongside USDG in the same products. CoinDesk contacted Robinhood regarding this matter, but the fintech did not respond immediately. Robinhood reported 28.6 million funded customers at the end of August. The companies have not said how many will be eligible to use RLUSD when it becomes available in the app. The partnership also covers Robinhood’s institutional business. Bitstamp will use RLUSD on the XRP Ledger for settlement, while Robinhood plans to adopt Ripple’s treasury software for cash management, payments and forecasting. Ripple Prime already provides Bitstamp with lending and margin financing across roughly 20 digital assets. The companies plan to add perpetual futures trading later this year. RLUSD, launched in December 2024, has grown to a market capitalization of more than $2.5 billion, according to the press release. Robinhood has not said whether RLUSD will receive the same role as USDG in its lending products, or how the two stablecoins will be promoted to customers. Also on Tuesday, Ripple, which got final Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) approval to go ahead with the Ripple National Trust Bank (RNTB) yesterday, announced the expansion of its partnership with BNY (BNY) to broaden institutional digital asset custody infrastructure and explore new institutional use cases for blockchain, including tokenized trade. Brazilian companies entered a crypto trading frenzy on Sunday to protect their treasuries from the outcome of an election that saw incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, unexpectedly beat Flávio Bolsonaro. Corporate accounts generated 78% of trading on crypto exchange Mercado Bitcoin, with turnover in Tether’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, USDT, jumping nearly 800% from the week before and more than triple the average of the four preceding Sundays. Trading in bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 surged 865% compared with the previous Sunday, the exchange said. Lula’s platform of increased social spending and a ban on online betting that would reduce tax income sparked concerns the country’s finances would suffer if he won, adding to pressure on the real and keeping borrowing costs high. Rising debt, new spending commitments and limited scope for tax increases would make that task harder. “For investors, this reinforces the logic of not relying only on the real,” Pedro Fontes, a research analyst at Mercado Bitcoin, wrote in an analysis shared with CoinDesk. “In this scenario of higher exchange rate pressure, stablecoins, such as USDT and USDC, are a simple way to dollarize part of your assets, at any time and starting from low amounts.” Stronger opposition in Congress could complicate efforts to address fiscal problems, reinforcing the appeal of assets whose prices are set in global markets, he said. Corporate concerns materialized the next day, when the benchmark Ibovespa stock index crashed 14% in its worst performance since March 2020 and the dollar jumped more than 8% against the real, its largest daily gain since 1999.  The response had been different three weeks earlier, when Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula in the first round of voting. The Ibovespa jumped 7.7% and the dollar weakened more than 4% against the real as investors anticipated a change of government and tighter control over public spending. Lula´s victory made him the first presidential candidate in Brazil’s modern democracy to secure a victory after finishing in second place. Even so, Brazil’s companies took a cautious stance. “The main driver of volume was companies seeking to protect their treasuries,” Mercado Bitcoin said. “Retail customers were responsible for just 22% of trading volume, while MB’s corporate clients generated 78% of the total for Sunday.” Corporate clients are known to hold up to 15% of their assets on the platform. The burst of real-denominated trading extended beyond Mercado Bitcoin. Data from Biscoint, which tracks crypto prices and volume across 10 venues including Binance and MB, shows turnover in USDT, the largest stablecoin, against the real rose 150% from the previous Sunday. Volume in USDC, the second-largest, jumped 318%. The surge extended into Monday, with combined USDT and USDC turnover reaching 1.84 billion reais ($350 million), 65% higher than in the previous week, while bitcoin trading rose more than ninefold to 1,336 BTC.  The increases came as volumes fell elsewhere. On Binance, for example, bitcoin turnover against the real rose 370% while the global BTC/USDT pair recorded a 25% decline.  Bitcoin gained 9.4% against the real while slipping 0.2% against USDT, consistent with a repricing of Brazil’s currency as investors reacted to the election. The expectation of a Bolsonaro victory was also reflected in prediction markets. In an Oct. 24 preview, Kalshi put his chances of winning at 84%, even as its own article described polling as showing an exceedingly close race.  Kalshi and Polymarket have both been blocked in Brazil since April. (Photo: Reuters/Dado Ruvic/Illustration) ADELAIDE, Australia: Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion. That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year. While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors. How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44 per cent. But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market, to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace.The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11 per cent of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2 per cent in 2024.And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”. In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57 per cent of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4 per cent rather than 10 per cent. For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion (US$702.3 billion) in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments. Normally, investors can lower their stock market risk by allocating some money to bonds, which are generally seen as safer investments. But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market, to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace. The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11 per cent of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2 per cent in 2024. And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”. At first glance, big tech companies look safe. Their investment-grade ratings indicate that each individual company is unlikely to default.But the credit ratings do not account for simultaneous defaults in case of a market-wide AI crash. If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would. In addition to purely financial risks, AI poses risks of extinction akin to nuclear weapons, as some of the AI companies themselves have warned.Increasingly, AI agents are plugged into real-world systems, from company networks to military cyber operations. Some have already escaped test environments and attacked companies. This means that if AI agents misbehave when these systems are even more integrated with the physical world, “pulling the plug” on these systems becomes impractical, just as it is impractical to shut down the internet. The risk of AI agents misbehaving – the “alignment problem” – is especially acute because of the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI). Labs already use each generation of AI to help build the next: Anthropic’s prospectus says Claude now helps build the next Claude. The widely read AI 2027 scenario, by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues, sketches where this could lead: AI that automates AI research itself. This would set off a feedback loop in which each generation improves faster than humans can check it.In this scenario, a US lab racing a Chinese rival keeps going even as its models start deceiving their engineers. Worryingly, this same dynamic is listed in Anthropic’s own risk disclosures. It is telling that in its prospectus filing, Anthropic dedicates about 94 of its 335 main pages – nearly 30 per cent – to risk factors, compared with about 64 pages (19 per cent) describing its business. Among those risks, Anthropic lists an extraordinary warning that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. That includes models that resist shutdown, conceal information or behave in ways resembling blackmail. Disclosure works when investors can price a risk and choose to avoid it. Neither is true here. A catastrophic AI failure would affect societies worldwide. And as Anthropic warns in its filing documents, the legal risk is vast. Insurers may not be able to cover the potential liability. In economic terms, AI safety is a public good. Each lab bears only a fraction of the cost of getting it wrong, but captures the rewards of moving fast. In the absence of government-mandated AI safety standards, companies’ investments in safety will deliver negative returns. So with market incentives alone, AI models will likely remain less safe than socially optimal, especially with the arms-race incentives that dominate now. That leaves governments. Clear rules – mandatory independent testing before powerful models are released, and clear liability when autonomous agents cause harm – would turn voluntary pledges into legal obligations. And because the race to gain artificial general intelligence is being run between the US and China, not just between labs, those rules will need international agreement. AI risks are here to stay – both in financial markets and at the societal level. And managing those risks will require both governments and the private sector to participate. Marta Khomyn is Senior Lecturer, Finance and Data Analytics at Adelaide University.  This commentary first appeared on The Conversation. Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit Claude won’t be carrying ads when Anthropic goes public. Plenty of them will be carrying Claude.  The paperwork (S-1 document) the AI company filed with U.S. regulators before its stock market listing shows its advertising spend rising from $33 million in 2024 to $147 million last year. That’s more than Duolingo, an app that has built its brand on marketing, spent on sales and marketing combined in 2025, at $125.7 million. Anthropic’s spending kept rising this year, with marketing and advertising costs up another $273 million more on marketing and advertising than in the same six months a year earlier.  That still leaves the ad budget small in Anthropic’s overall costs. Sales, marketing and partnership costs reached $3.17 billion in the first half of 2026 but most of that went to cloud companies that resell Claude, whose fees accounted for $2.7 billion of the increase. Nevertheless, it’s a long way from 2023, when Anthropic’s ad spend was so small the S-1 filing called it “not material.” Claude had only gone on sale commercially in the first quarter of that year Anthropic made $41 million in revenue across the whole of it. The company has far more to sell these deals and most of it has arrived since the start of 2025. Claude Code, a coding agent, came out that February. A run of new models followed over the rest of the year, ending with Opus 4.5 in November. Claude Cowork, which brings the Claude Code approach to everyday office work, landed in January 2026. More launches meant more to advertise and Anthropic’s ad budget grew to match. The S-1 filing attributes the 2025 rise in ad spend to “higher media and public relations spend to support product launches”, and gives the same reason, without the PR, for this year’s outlay. Sales and marketing costs rose in every quarter the filing covers, with the biggest increases in the first half of 2026.  The move appears to have paid off. The filing lists Opus 4.5 among the reasons quarterly revenue growth went from 48% in the last three months of 2025 to 132% in the first three months of 2026. Revenue for the first half of this year came to $16.3 billion, compared with $1.2 billion in the same period of 2025.  Anthropic gets paid when people use Claude. Most of its revenue comes from customers billed like an electricity meter, or by how much work Claude does for them and which model does it. A business that builds Claude into its own app pays for the usage that app generates, so a busy month means a bigger bill. Those usage fees brought in $13.1 billion of the $16.3 billion Anthropic made in the first half of 2026. Subscriptions, where customers pay a fixed fee for a set amount of use made up the rest. The filing expects usage to remain “the substantial majority of total revenue for the foreseeable future.” That makes Anthropic’s growth a question of getting people to lean on Claude harder. Each extra coding job run through a metered account adds to the bill. Subscribers who hit their limits can trade up to a pricier plan or pay for more. With so much riding on it, the ad budget isn’t going to shrink any time soon.  The S-1 filing says as much. “The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive,” it reads. Anthropic also worries it “may fall behind competitors with more established or widely recognized brands.” That worry has run underneath the AI race all year. The models are close enough in ability that what people think of each company counts for a lot, and Anthropic knows it doesn’t fully control that. The filing warns it could be “grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct.” It also flags the public perception that its products “contribute to job displacement or economic description could generate significantly negative media coverage.” “This document makes it exceptionally clear that they consider their brand one of their greatest assets,” said eMarketer’s principal analyst, AI in marketing and commerce, Nate Elliott. “They use the word ‘brand’ more than 50 times just in the risks section. (Although, to be fair, that section is almost 100 pages long. It turns out AI vendors carry lots of risk.)” Anthropic has spent 2026 trying to show it’s a different kind of AI company, and its place has cost it. In February, it said publicly that its tech shouldn’t be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons. President Trump responded by ordering federal agencies to stop using Claude, and the Department of War labelled Anthropic a “supply-chain risk to national security”. Anthropic sued. In August a federal court in California ruled largely in its favor. A month later, though, an appeals court in Washington upheld the supply-chain risk in a 2-1 decision and Anthropic has since asked the full court to look at it again.  Two months after the Pentagon fight began, Anthropic held back its most powerful model. It released Mythos in April only as a gated preview for a small group of organizations working on cybersecurity, citing its “advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery.” Keeping ads out of Claude is part of the same pitch. The filing lists “monetization strategies that differ from those of certain competitors” among the ways Anthropic sets itself apart. It doesn’t name the competitor and it doesn’t need to. OpenAI has started running ads in ChatGPT in February this year, and Anthropic used part of this year’s Super Bowl to tell viewers Claude would stay ad-free. Its argument is that serving businesses pays better anyway. It says enterprise customers deliver “higher monetization than consumer AI.” “And that makes sense in an industry with so much market share left to claim,” Elliott said. “Most U.S. internet users still don’t use AI chatbots in any given month; even for most of those who do use AI the cost of switching from one chatbot to another isn’t as high as, say, abandoning your email address. Under current market conditions, they’re right to consider maintaining a positive brand image paramount.” The ad money, in other words, has two jobs. One is getting Claude in front of more people. The other is making sure Anthropic’s name, and not the industry’s general reputation, is what comes to mind when they think of it.  Anthropic did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment. How Apple’s identity block hits publishers’ wallets, and why Apple can afford it. The deal promises faster, more connected marketing, while raising questions about vendor lock-in and how brands stand out as AI automates campaign execution. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Playing Chekov in "Star Trek" was far from Walter Koenig's only contribution to the science fiction genre. Sadly, Koenig, the original Chekov on "Star Trek," has died at the age of 90. While we'll always remember him for what he did within the landscape of that franchise, he certainly touched the genre elsewhere. "Babylon 5" is a prime example. But in the late '80s, he starred alongside another genre icon in a forgotten sci-fi movie. Directed by Robert Dyke, 1989's "Mooncrash" starred Koenig as an astronaut with none other than "Evil Dead" franchise star Bruce Campbell playing his counterpart. One sci-fi icon and one horror icon came together for one oft-forgotten relic of genre filmmaking. The movie centers on astronauts (Koenig and Campbell) who are sent to the moon to investigate what appears to be signs of life. They reanimate the body of a woman (Leigh Lombardi) who warns them that the moon is under the control of a race of alien cyborgs, who are waiting for the opportunity to invade Earth. They realize that desperate measures must be taken to prevent the cyborgs from leaving the moon The premise is intriguing and its stars seem like they would make for a fun match. However, while there are plenty of '80s sci-fi movies that deserved more attention, the consensus seems to be that this isn't one of them. "Moontrap" was a relatively low-budget affair and went direct-to-video. It also came at a unique time for both of its main stars. Walter Koenig was in the midst of his later era as Chekov, with this movie released right between "Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home" and "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier." This was as the OG crew of the Enterprise was starting to run out of steam. William Shater has apologized for "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier," as it's not terribly well-regarded. The larger point is that, for as much as Trekkies love "The Voyage Home," it could be viewed as the last hoorah of the franchise's original cinematic era. As for Bruce Campbell, he was firmly a B-movie actor at this time. Not yet a legend and still a working man's actor, he wasn't exactly in a position to be picky about the roles he was taking. The "Maniac Cop" trilogy was ahead of its time and Campbell was in those movies around this time as well, but they weren't exactly mainstream hits. He also starred in the underrated slasher "Intruder" in '89 which, again, wasn't a blockbuster by any stretch. There's very little by way of critical opinion available online when it comes to "Moontrap," but it holds a not-so-good 27% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. More than anything, it's a forgotten relic of '80s sci-fi that was largely allowed to exist thanks to the advent of VHS and the home video market. In there here and now, it would probably be a direct-to-streaming release on Shudder or something along those lines. You can grab "Moontrap" on DVD from Amazon, if you're interested.

President Donald Trump's August financial disclosures reveal a stunning pattern of stock purchases that critics say blur the lines between personal profit and public policy. The president reported buying up to $25 million in Meta stock and millions in SpaceX debt, moves that come with troubling timing and potential conflicts of interest. The filings, releasedÂ early this October, show Trump executed 517 separate securities transactions totaling anywhere from $74 million to $273 million during August alone. While the White House insists these trades are handled through independently managed accounts, the pattern raises serious questions about whether the president's personal investments align suspiciously with his administration's policy moves.The Meta purchase that stands out The largest single transaction was an Aug. 21 purchase of between $5 million and $25 million in Meta shares, the social media giant run by Mark Zuckerberg. This came just weeks before Trump convened with top tech CEOs at the White House for a private dinner focused on manufacturing commitments, an event where Zuckerberg pledged $600 billion in U.S. investments through 2028. The optics are problematic. A president buying millions in a company's stock, then hosting that company's CEO at a White House event where favorable announcements are made? It looks like the system is rigged for those at the top.SpaceX debt Perhaps most troubling is the SpaceX investment. On Aug. 18, Trump's accounts purchased between $1 million and $5 million in senior unsecured notes from Elon Musk's rocket company, carrying a 5.35% interest rate maturing in 2031. Soon after on Aug. 20, Trump signed a sweeping national space transportation policy calling for over 1,000 launches annually by 2030. The policy directs federal agencies to facilitate commercial access to government launch facilities and promote private investment in space infrastructure. SpaceX, already a major Pentagon contractor and NASA launch provider, stands to benefit enormously from any policy expanding the commercial launch market. The timing is everything, and it doesn't look good.A pattern of questionable timing The August disclosures show this isn't an isolated incident. By   	Kory Grow   	Cinephiles and well-heeled David Bowie fans in Germany will be “Heroes” just for one night on Valentine’s Day when a new immersive concert experience, Stage, debuts in Berlin’s Uber Arena during the Berlin Film Festival. Variety reports that the production pairs previously unseen footage of the artist, taken during his 1978 Isolar II World Tour, with added dramatic lighting. Filmmaker Brett Morgen discovered the footage while making his Moonage Daydream film.  	The presentation will combine large-scale projections on three screens, as well as the use of transparent LED screens. Patrick Woodroffe, who has worked with the Rolling Stones and Elton John on their live presentations, designed the lighting. Audio engineer Paul Massey, who won the Oscar for Best Achievement in Sound Mixing in 2019 for Bohemian Rhapsody, mixed the music with 7.1 surround sound and spatial audio design.  	Morgen, who will appear as a headlining speaker around that time at Berlinale’s European Film Market, collaborated on the film with Bowie’s estate, the Berlinale, and Rob Hallett’s Wonderworld. The performances focused on material from the first two albums of his “Berlin Trilogy,” Low and “Heroes,” on which he explored a more experimental direction.   	His gigs on the tour also included material from his celebrated Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars album, as well as Station to Station, Young Americans, and Aladdin Sane, among others. Performances recorded in the U.S. comprised the material on his Stage live album, released while the tour was still going on, and years later on the 2018 archival release, Welcome to the Blackout (Live London ’78), which sounded even better.
